context.text: Militia companies were clubs for Amsterdam's powerful burghers, and group portraits of their members conventionally posed the men in static rows around a table. Rembrandt broke the convention: his company of harquebusiers surges into action, marching out of a gateway around Captain Frans Banninck Cocq and his lieutenant. The men paid to appear — about a hundred guilders from each of the junior sitters, roughly sixteen hundred in all — and the shield above the gate lists eighteen of their names.

The nickname is a mistake that stuck. The scene is daytime; the picture only became 'The Night Watch' in the nineteenth century, when its varnish had browned almost to darkness (the layer was removed in 1975). The legend that the sitters rejected the picture is equally spurious: there is no sign anyone depicted was unhappy, and Banninck Cocq was pleased enough to commission two copies.

details.text: The captain's outstretched hand throws a shadow across the lieutenant's yellow coat — and the shadow of his thumb and finger lands exactly on the embroidered lion holding Amsterdam's three-cross arms.
The glowing girl in yellow carries a dead fowl with conspicuously large claws at her belt: a pun-mascot for the company, since klovenier (harquebusier) sounds like klauwenier, from klauw, 'claw'.
The picture is incomplete: a strip at the left containing three figures was cut away in the eighteenth century.

context.text: Seurat showed this canvas at the eighth and final impressionist exhibition in 1886, where it marked a schism: in the critic Félix Fénéon's words, Degas and the older generation showed characteristic work while 'Pissarro, Seurat, and Signac innovate'. Fénéon championed the picture, explained its technique in minutely scientific terms, and coined a name for what it began — neo-impressionism.

Seurat had considered the painting finished by spring 1885, then reworked it after a summer at Grandcamp, applying for the first time the 'optical mixture' at the heart of his method — small touches of pure colour set side by side, left for the eye to blend.

details.text: The composition was built, not glimpsed: it rests on a long campaign of preparatory work, from conté crayon drawings to small oil studies on wood, several now in museum collections themselves.

context.text: The seemingly informal scene — a court portrait at this scale behaving like a snapshot of studio life — was something new in art. Velázquez, Philip IV's favourite painter and eventually his chamberlain, shows himself at work on a huge canvas while the five-year-old Infanta Margarita and her two maids of honour (the meninas of the title) occupy the foreground. It stands as one of the most subtle and powerful experiments in representation in Western art.

The key hangs at the back of the room: the mirror reflecting Philip IV and his queen. They are posing for the portrait Velázquez is painting — which places us, the viewers, exactly where the king and queen stand. De Rynck reads the game with levels of reality as a deliberate argument, fiercely current at the time, that painting is more than a craft.

details.text: At the right, the jester Nicolasito slyly rests his foot on the drowsing dog, while the dwarf Mari-Bárbola's stocky figure sets off the Infanta's fragility.
The red cross of the Order of Santiago on the painter's chest is a small anachronism: Velázquez was not admitted to the order until two or three years after the picture was painted.

context.text: On one level this is the least complex of Vermeer's paintings — no background, no setting, no story, just a young woman turning toward us out of darkness. The bareness is the point: whatever a Vermeer ostensibly shows, its true subject is light, and here light is given almost nothing else to do.

details.text: The picture's whole effect balances on three small highlights: the shimmer on the pearl, the brightness of the eye, and the gleam of moisture on the parted lower lip.

context.text: Giovanni Arnolfini was an Italian merchant from Lucca who spent years in Bruges, where van Eyck served the Burgundian court. The picture was long read as the record of a wedding or betrothal — van Eyck as 'a notary with a paintbrush' — but that reading has been seriously questioned: the man's gesture is not the affirmation of marriage vows it was once taken for, and the panel keeps much of its enigma.

details.text: The convex mirror shows the missing quarter of the room — two figures standing where we stand, one perhaps the painter himself. Above it runs the conspicuous Latin inscription 'Johannes de eyck fuit hic. 1434': Jan van Eyck was here.

The furnishings double as symbols, on period conventions: the little dog for fidelity, the cast-off clogs, the single lit candle in the chandelier, oranges suggesting both prosperity and prelapsarian innocence — and around the mirror frame, tiny medallions of the Passion of Christ.

context.text: Jean de Dinteville, French ambassador to London (aged 29 — his dagger sheath says so), commissioned this record of the 1533 visit of his friend Georges de Selve, bishop of Lavaur (aged 25 — inscribed on the book under his elbow). It is among the earliest portraits to pose two full-length figures at the scale of life. The pair are commonly read as the active and the contemplative life personified, with the instruments between them a compendium of the culture of their age.

details.text: The smear across the floor resolves, viewed from the right edge of the panel, into a perfectly drawn skull — an anamorphosis. It is the quintessential memento mori (Dinteville's own cap badge carries a skull), and a hint that the world's appearances must be looked at correctly to yield their meaning.

The still life keeps up the argument: a lute with one snapped string (a traditional emblem of fragility), a hymnal open at Luther's 'Come Holy Ghost', and — half-hidden by the green hanging in the top left corner — a crucifix.

context.text: Begin with the shock of it: nothing like this near-life-size female nude had been seen in Europe for a thousand years. Botticelli was a renowned painter of Madonnas in a culture where almost ninety percent of pictures were religious; at the peak of his career he painted four large mythologies from the pagan classics, of which this is one — often counted the first large-scale Renaissance painting with an exclusively secular, mythological subject.

Before her, the only female nudes art had dared were Eves, stooping in shame at the expulsion. Botticelli's Venus instead revives the classical canon of Polyclitus and Praxiteles — the weight on one leg, the curve of the hip, the chaste gesture — proportions the Renaissance had just rediscovered and that have shaped taste ever since.

details.text: The tempera's boldness is recent news: a later coat of varnish had aged to yellow-brown, and its removal in the restoration finished in 1987 returned the sky, waves and figures to their original brightness.

context.text: Painted in Titian's thirties for the studiolo of Alfonso d'Este in the castle of Ferrara, where the duke was recreating an ancient picture gallery described in a late-antique Greek text. Alfonso had wanted the best painters in Italy — Fra Bartolommeo and Raphael both died with only drawings done, and their commissions reverted to Titian.

The story, rarely painted before, comes from Ovid and Catullus — translated extracts were sent to Titian along with the canvas and stretchers. Ariadne, abandoned on Naxos by Theseus (his ship is still on the horizon at the left), is surprised by Bacchus leaping from his cheetah-drawn chariot; the constellation she will become already hangs in the sky above her.

details.text: The blue half of the picture is an expanse of ultramarine among the costliest pigments of the age, available in this range only in Venice; against it the maenad clashing cymbals glows in a tunic of orange realgar, Ariadne's mirror image across the picture's earthy half.
Titian's small dog barks at the strutting faun trailing a mangled calf's head — beside it, a caper flower, a symbol of love.

context.text: At the Salon of 1865 this picture caused one of the most documented scandals in art. Room M was so crowded one could hardly move; reviewers described laughter, catcalls and astonishment that the jury had admitted it at all, and Manet never fully escaped the reputation of 'the painter of Olympia'. Manet wrote to Baudelaire that insults were raining on him — and received the bracing reply that he was hardly the first.

What the critics saw as incompetence — 'the colour of the flesh is dirty, the modelling non-existent', shadows 'indicated by more or less large smears of blacking' — was precisely the flat, hard manner that made the picture modern.

details.text: Contemporaries fixed on the same three presences: the nude with her unapologetic gaze, the maid carrying a bouquet, and the black cat at the foot of the bed — 'is it a cat, really?', Baudelaire relayed from an early viewer.
In the Salon catalogue Manet attached five lines of verse by Zacharie Astruc naming Olympia — a name that for 1865 readers carried the echo, as Gautier noted, of a notorious Renaissance courtesan.

context.text: Read left to right, the triptych argues: a true paradise where Christ blesses the union of Adam and Eve; a false paradise of naked pleasure-seekers; and the hell those pleasures earn. De Rynck reads it as a hallucinatory warning — the core message that sexual passion threatens the soul — delivered, in true Boschian fashion, through the most profane images imaginable.

details.text: In the central panel, men ride in an endless circle around women bathing in a pond — the animals they ride standing for their passions, and riding in a circle itself, in the literature of Bosch's time, a figure of sinfulness.
An owl peers from the globe of the plant-like Fountain of Life in the left panel: in Bosch's vocabulary an image of dark, seductive evil, planted in paradise from the start.

context.text: Bruegel was nicknamed 'Peasant Bruegel' for his subjects, but he was a man of the highest sophistication, and pictures like this one rank him among the greatest landscape painters of all time. The scene is not his flat Netherlands but an invented northern world seen from a great height — its power owing much to his engagement with mapping, the seasons theme joined to an extensive mapped view of the earth.

details.text: The vertical trees march the eye down the hill with the hunters, whose weary dogs follow thin and dejected; it may be the coldest painting ever made.

Everyone in the valley is absorbed in getting through winter — the family roasting a pig by the inn, the tiny skaters enclosed in their occupations — and no one but us sees the astounding beauty spread out below.

context.text: The Temeraire had distinguished herself at Trafalgar in 1805; by the 1830s the veteran warships of the Napoleonic wars were being replaced by steam. Turner encountered the old ship on a Thames excursion, sold out of the service and under tow from Sheerness to Rotherhithe to be scrapped, and exhibited the picture at the Royal Academy in 1839 with lines from Thomas Campbell: 'The flag which braved the battle and the breeze / No longer owns her.'

The picture reads as an elegy staged like a modern Claude: a heroic and graceful age passing with the dying sun, a petty age of steam and money rising with the pale moon — and the last berth recalling the breaking up of every human life.

details.text: The ghostly, moonlit ship against the squat black tug belching fire is a deliberate manipulation — topography and shipbuilding alike are bent to symbolic ends rather than documentary truth.
Look at the surface itself: thickly impastoed rays and reflections in the sunset against thinly painted passages, with colour swooping abruptly from light to dark.

context.text: These pictures set out to record how the world looks rather than to stage an event. The more closely a painter attends to the surface of things, the less room is left for anything to happen: the figures are held still to be looked at, Vermeer's above all.
That is also how the art was valued for most of its history. Before the twentieth century, writers treated these pictures as a description of Holland and of Dutch life.

These painters describe the world instead of telling a story about it. The detail rewards a long view and a very close one at the same time, and the people are held still to be looked at rather than caught mid-action: the more carefully a painter attends to how things look, the less room is left for anything to happen.

Calling that static applies an Italian yardstick, one that expected a painting to tell a story and to move the viewer by telling it. Measured that way, description looks like a failure to narrate — which is why pictures of this kind were long dismissed as either meaningless or second-rate.

The culmination of the Renaissance is conventionally placed in the two decades from about 1500, when Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael produced the works that have been treated for centuries as touchstones of perfection.
Florence had been pre-eminent throughout the fifteenth century, but by the sixteenth Rome and Venice were centres of equal importance.

Florence is reasonably seen as the cradle of the Renaissance, and the years around 1425 — when Masaccio, Brunelleschi and Donatello were making some of their most inventive work — as a turning point in European art.

'Renaissance' means rebirth, and named a revival of the values of the classical world. Almost no ancient painting survived to imitate, but classical painters were known from ancient writers to have excelled at fidelity to nature, so that became the keynote; Masaccio brought a new scientific rigour to the problems of representation.

The word comes from the Italian maniera, style or stylishness, and Vasari used it as praise — for grace, poise, facility and sophistication. Later critics turned it into an accusation, reading the art of Vasari's generation as a decline from the High Renaissance into artificiality and exaggeration. Only in the twentieth century did it settle into a neutral period label.

The qualities usually meant by it: tension and emotionalism, elongated figures and strained poses, unusual effects of scale, lighting or perspective, and vivid — sometimes harsh — colour, with the artist often drawing attention to his own virtuosity.

The dominant style of European art between Mannerism and Rococo. It originated in Rome and is bound up with the Catholic Counter-Reformation: its fervent rhetoric and dynamic movement suited a church that had recovered its confidence and meant to persuade.

Caravaggio and Annibale Carracci stand at the head of the tradition, taking movement and intense emotion from Mannerism and solidity and grandeur from the Renaissance. It is not an exclusively religious style — the same energy runs through the dynamic lines of Dutch still life.

A movement that began in France in the 1860s. It was never a formal group with a programme, but a loose association linked by outlook, who banded together to exhibit after most of them had trouble getting work accepted for the official Salon; they held eight shows in Paris between 1874 and 1886.

What united them was a rebellion against academic convention: catching an impression of what the eye sees at a particular moment rather than a detailed record, most often landscape and often painted outdoors, in bright colour and sketchy brushwork that struck traditionalists as bewildering. The name was coined derisively by the critic Louis Leroy, from Monet's Impression: Sunrise at the first exhibition.

Venice was the other great centre of Italian art, second in importance only to Florence — proud, prosperous, and with trade that linked it closely to the East. It took the Renaissance style later than other Italian cities, and when it did the style acquired a new gaiety, splendour and warmth.

Its painters handled colour more deliberately and more observantly than anyone else in Italy, and the place itself may be the reason: the air over the lagoons softens the outlines of things and blends their colours in a radiant light.

The achievements of the Italian masters made a deep impression north of the Alps, where artists suddenly found their own work looking old-fashioned by comparison. Three Italian gains were concrete enough to point at: scientific perspective, a knowledge of anatomy and so of the human body, and the classical forms of building.
Northern artists answered that new knowledge in very different ways — some absorbing it, some holding out against it, a few swamped by it.

'Renaissance' means rebirth: a revival of the values of the classical world, claimed as early as the fifteenth century by Italians who believed ancient art and literature were blossoming again after centuries of barbarism.

The label later stretched from a cultural movement into a period, and has come to mark the point where medieval turns into modern — a religion-dominated world giving way to a culture more concerned with the individual. Modern historians treat that as gradual change rather than a clean break.

Too varied to define in a sentence, but its keynote was a belief in the value of individual experience — a reaction against the rationalism of the Enlightenment and the orderliness of Neoclassicism, trading public discourse for a more private kind of expression.
It is usually set against classicism, though the two share more than the opposition suggests: both are concerned with the ideal rather than the real, and both embrace nobility, grandeur and virtue.
The dominant movement in European art and architecture of the period, driven by a wish to recreate the spirit and the forms of ancient Greece and Rome.

A newly scientific interest in classical antiquity fed it — the excavations at Pompeii began in 1748, with Herculaneum alongside — and it is also read as a reaction against the light-hearted frivolity of the Rococo. The order, clarity and reason of Greek and Roman art were the appeal.

A style of lightness, grace, playfulness and intimacy that emerged in France around 1700. The name was coined derisively around 1796 by a pupil of David, combining rocaille with barocco, and long carried a sense of the excessively florid; it is now used without the sneer.

It was both a development from the Baroque and a reaction against it. It kept the love of complex form but dropped the concern with solidity and mass in favour of delicate play across the surface, sombre colour and heavy gilding giving way to lighter tones.

The name a group of young English artists took in 1848, out of dismay at what they saw as the moribund state of British painting. They wanted to recover the sincerity and simplicity of early Italian art — before Raphael, whom they blamed as the source of academicism.
The nucleus was three Royal Academy students: Millais, Holman Hunt and Rossetti, whose idea the secret Brotherhood was. The movement had a strong literary flavour from the start.

Not a style but a generation, and they varied enormously. Cézanne wanted 'to make of Impressionism something solid and enduring, like the art of the museums'; Gauguin renounced 'the abominable error of naturalism' for the symbolic use of colour and line; van Gogh's emotional intensity became the fountainhead of Expressionism. Seurat, of almost equal importance, went the other way, into a scientific analysis of colour.
The drift of the whole group was away from Impressionist naturalism and towards the avant-garde movements — Fauvism, Cubism — that transformed European art in the decade before the First World War.

The painting technique associated with Seurat and his followers: colour laid down in small separate touches. It is often confused with divisionism, but divisionism refers mainly to the underlying colour theory while pointillism describes the actual handling.

A loosely organised movement in literature and art that gave up direct, literal representation for evocation and suggestion. It belonged to a broad turn against materialism at the end of the nineteenth century, and was aimed specifically at the naturalism of Impressionism.

Symbolist painters tried to give visual form to emotional experience, or as Jean Moréas put it in the 1886 manifesto, 'to clothe the idea in sensuous form'. Colour and line were held to express ideas and feelings in themselves.
Distortion and exaggeration used for emotional effect: art that puts what the artist feels above what the eye reports. In that broad sense it reaches back to Grünewald and El Greco.
Narrowly, it names a trend in modern European art using strong unnaturalistic colour and distorted or abbreviated form to project inner feeling — a line that begins with van Gogh.

Hudson River school.name: Hudson River School
Hudson River school.places: New York State and New England

context.text: A name applied retrospectively to American landscape painters inspired by pride in the beauty of their own country — Thomas Cole, Thomas Doughty and Asher B. Durand foremost — who painted the Hudson River Valley, the Catskills and other untouched places.

Most had studied in Europe, and part of the inspiration came from painters of the grandiose and spectacular such as Turner and John Martin. Their patriotic spirit made them very popular in mid-century.

Painting made inside a sophisticated society but without conventional training in representational skill. Colour tends to be bright and unnaturalistic, perspective unscientific, and the vision childlike or literal-minded.

'Primitive' is sometimes used as a synonym and is best avoided — it also gets applied to pre-Renaissance painting and to the art of societies called uncivilised. 'Folk art' and 'Sunday painter' have their own pitfalls.

Capitalised, it names a movement in nineteenth-century art, French above all: a revolt against the historical, mythological and religious subjects painting was supposed to take, in favour of unidealised scenes of modern life. Courbet led it, insisting that painting is 'essentially a concrete art' and must deal with real and existing things.

The lowercase word is far looser, close to naturalism: any wish to show things accurately and objectively. Even then it usually carries a refusal of conventionally beautiful subjects, and often a preference for low life or for ordinary people at work.

The spirit of order, clarity and harmony long associated with the art of ancient Greece and Rome. Used broadly, it names the opposite of Romanticism: art that keeps to recognised ideals of beauty rather than pressing the individuality of the artist.

It need not involve copying antique art, though that is often implied. Depending on who is using it, the word can mean little more than that a picture is clear — or, less kindly, that it is conservative.

academic art.name: Academic art
academic art.span: 17th–19th century, at its height in 19th-century France
academic art.places: The Paris Salon, and academies across Europe

context.text: Painting made in the tradition of the official academies, whose teaching and whose Salon juries defined what serious art should look like. The Academy ranked its genres and defended the ranking: it was wary of encouraging landscape far enough to threaten the standing of history painting.

The modern contempt for this art is increasingly treated as a position with an agenda of its own. Writers championing the avant-garde had an interest in running the academies down, and doing so hid how much the modernists owed to the training they had received there.

Orientalism.name: Orientalism
Orientalism.places: French and British painters; subjects from North Africa and the Near East

context.text: European painting of North Africa and the Near East, which flourished alongside the height of European colonial expansion in the nineteenth century. What its painters shared, on the standard account, was the aim of documentary realism.

Such pictures are now generally read against the empire that produced them. Gérôme's Snake Charmer, on this reading, distils a Western idea of the East and then presents it in the language of plain fact. The realism is the part to be wary of: it reports one side's version of a place as simply how things were.
It was also a commercial success: Fromentin, Lewis, Gérôme and Decamps commanded high prices, enough that popular compositions were frequently repeated as copies and variants.

Between about 1880 and 1914, European culture came to feel decisively modern. Machinery was remaking daily life and a new century was arriving, and the mood around both ran close to millenarian: the future turned into something people believed in.

The ending was bureaucratic rather than dramatic. By the 1970s modernism was the official culture of Europe and America — settled into the museums, paid for by corporations and government agencies — and the idea of an avant-garde had quietly stopped meaning anything.

The greatest painter of the Venetian school, with the career to match: some sixty years at the top of it. He probably trained under Giovanni Bellini and fell early under Giorgione's spell, but Giorgione died in 1510 and Bellini in 1516, and after that nobody in Venice stood above him.

He worked almost entirely in oils. His first securely dated works are frescos painted in Padua in 1511, and although they show he could handle the medium he hardly touched it again. In his last decades he painted mainly for patrons outside Venice, which left Tintoretto and Veronese the run of the city.

He came to painting at twenty-seven, after failing as a picture dealer, a teacher, and a lay preacher among Belgian miners. That left him ten years, and in them he made about a thousand paintings and as many drawings again, kept going almost entirely by his brother Theo, who sent money, materials and prints from Paris.
The wild and unreasoning side of him gets most of the attention, but he was well read and thought hard about his pictures. Fast as he worked, he planned them carefully.

Of the painters of the High Renaissance he is the one who expresses its ideals most completely. He was born in Urbino to a painter attached to its humanist court, and grew up with a cultivation that most artists of the day lacked — he was known for his social poise, and it served him well with patrons for the whole of his career.

His father died when he was eleven and nothing is documented about his training, but Perugino shaped the early work more than anyone else did: the sweetness of expression and the elegance come from him. Raphael was dead at thirty-seven.

About seventy of his pictures survive and he was dead at thirty-eight, yet no Italian painter of the seventeenth century counted for more. He swept aside the prevailing Mannerism for something blunt and naturalistic: solid, flesh-and-blood figures pushed up to the front of the picture, lit hard, standing against a dark ground with almost no depth behind them.

That realism was what got him into trouble. Several major altarpieces were refused as indecorous or theologically wrong — his Death of the Virgin shows her as a plainly believable corpse, and the church that had commissioned it sent it back — though collectors snapped up the rejected pictures almost at once.

His life ran alongside the work. He built up a long record for assault and insult in Rome, then killed a man in 1606 in a fight over a bet on a tennis match. He spent his last four years a fugitive, picking up important commissions in Naples, Malta and Sicily as he went, and died of fever on the road back to Rome, where he believed a pardon was waiting.

The greatest Baroque painter in northern Europe, and the most worldly. His style was formed in Italy, where he spent eight years from 1600 working for the Duke of Mantua, copying in the principal art centres and taking in antique sculpture, the Renaissance masters and Annibale Carracci. He came home to Antwerp in 1608, was court painter within a year, and never saw Italy again.

Demand was so great that he could only meet it by running a very efficient studio. He collaborated with established painters and retouched work by pupils, and what a picture cost reflected how much of it was his own hand — assistants generally carried it from the first oil sketch to the master's finishing touches. Van Dyck was the most distinguished of them.

He was also a working diplomat. Sent by the Spanish governors of the Netherlands to help end hostilities between Spain and England, he was knighted by the kings of both countries; he had Flemish, Italian, French, German, Latin and Spanish, which made him useful. In his last years he bought a country house between Brussels and Malines and took up landscape.

The greatest painter of the Spanish school, and one of the supreme portraitists anywhere. He was precocious: still in his teens in Seville he was painting with complete technical command, following his teacher Pacheco's advice to go to nature for everything, so that the figures in his religious pictures look like portraits rather than ideal types.

In 1623 he painted Philip IV, who liked the portrait enough to make him a court painter and to rule that nobody else should paint him. Velázquez was twenty-four, and he held the king's favour unchallenged for the rest of his life. From then on he was mainly a portraitist, and his palette lightened and his brushwork opened out, largely from studying the Titians in the royal collection.

The most powerful and original European artist of his time, though he was slow arriving: he was well into his thirties before he made anything that set him apart from his contemporaries. The son of a gilder, he trained with a local painter in Saragossa, failed twice to get into the Academy of San Fernando, and settled in Madrid in 1774.

His first steady employment was designing tapestries for the royal factory, which took most of his working time from 1775 to 1780; he made sixty-three in all. They are finished oil paintings rather than sketches, some more than twenty feet wide, and their idyllic and everyday subjects are handled with Rococo charm — but a sardonic streak already runs through them that points at the work to come.

He lived his whole life in Delft and rarely travelled even locally, made little mark while he was alive, and then spent two centuries in obscurity; among Dutch painters only Rembrandt now outranks him. Nobody knows who taught him. Only about thirty-five to forty of his paintings are known, and the number was probably never much higher.

He almost certainly earned most of his living some other way: his father kept an inn and dealt in pictures, and Vermeer very likely inherited both trades. It was not enough. Eleven of his fifteen children outlived him, the French invasion of 1672 wrecked the Dutch economy, and his widow was declared insolvent the year after he died.

Most of the pictures show one or two figures in a room lit from the viewer's left, occupied with something domestic, in yellows, blues and greys. They are small, and the composition and the handling of light give them a weight out of all proportion to their size. In reproduction the surface looks smooth and detailed; in fact he often laid the paint on broadly, varying the texture to catch the play of light.

One of the giants of nineteenth-century art, and an unlikely rebel. He was the son of a senior civil servant, inherited money, cut an impeccable figure about town, and wanted official honours all his life. His style owed less to his teacher Couture than to the Old Masters in the Louvre, and above all to Velázquez, whom he revered.

The scandals came anyway. The Salon rejected Déjeuner sur l'herbe in 1863 and it was shown among the refusés; the objection was moral as much as artistic, since a nude was acceptable only at a safe distance in time or place, and here a naked woman picnics with two clothed men of the day. Olympia caused worse two years later. The technique drew fire as well — he had dropped the fine tonal gradations of academic practice for stark contrasts of light and shade.

He led the avant-garde reluctantly. The young Impressionists admired him and he met them at the Café Guerbois, but he kept his distance and never showed in their exhibitions, though he did take up painting out of doors and his work grew lighter through the 1870s. Syphilis caught up with him at the end; he turned to pastel because it was less tiring than oils, and died a week after a gangrenous leg was amputated. The honours he had wanted arrived in 1881, too late to enjoy.

The archetypal Impressionist: his devotion to the movement's ideals never wavered across a very long career, and it was his Impression: Sunrise that gave the group its name. Boudin turned him from caricature to landscape and gave him the taste for working out of doors; of Jongkind he said he owed him the real education of his eye.

He liked to keep up the image of an outdoor painter. Women in the Garden stands about eight feet high, and to paint all of it outside he had a trench dug so the canvas could be raised and lowered on pulleys; he would not touch the leaves in the background unless the light was exactly right. In later life he leaned more and more on studio work.

From 1890 he worked in series, painting one subject over and over at different hours and in different light — the grainstacks first, then Rouen Cathedral. At Giverny he made a water garden, and from 1899 the waterlilies took his work over completely. His eyesight began to fail in 1908 and he had a cataract operation in 1923, but he painted to the end.

Cretan by birth and Spanish by choice, and reckoned the first great genius of the Spanish school. He signed his pictures Domenikos Theotokopoulos, in Greek characters, his whole life; Spain found the name unmanageable and called him simply the Greek. The odd hybrid 'El Greco' — a Spanish article on an Italian noun — took hold only after his death.

He came out of the Byzantine icon tradition, moved to Venice around 1567, and was in Rome by late 1570. Of the Venetians it was Tintoretto who marked him most, with his sense of movement and dramatic lighting. He won no public commissions in Italy and worked on a small scale; nothing from those years hints at what happened once he reached Spain.

He settled in Toledo in 1577 and stayed for the rest of his life. It was then the spiritual capital of Spain, with more than a hundred religious establishments, so the work came to him — a run of great altarpieces, and late paintings in which the figures come free of the ground altogether. The elongated bodies and irrational space have something in common with Italian Mannerism, but the flame-like forms, electric colour and ecstatic feeling are his alone.

The greatest artist of his time in northern Europe, and among the most misread. Almost everything known about him comes from a biography published in 1604, which fixed him as 'Pieter the Droll' — a comic painter, few of whose works could be looked at with a straight face. There is humour in them, but there is horror and tragedy too, and the indifference of natural forces.

'Peasant' Bruegel is wrong as well. He painted village life memorably, but he spent his career in major cities rather than the countryside, he had distinguished patrons, and he was a friend of the geographer Abraham Ortelius. Crossing the Alps on the way back from Italy affected him far more than any art he saw there — the mountains keep reappearing in his landscapes for years afterwards.

He moved to Brussels in 1563, and in the six years left to him worked mainly as a painter rather than a designer of prints. Nearly all his best-known pictures date from those years, among them the six paintings of The Months made for an Antwerp banker in 1565, five of which survive.

His country's greatest artist. The son of a prosperous miller, he attended Leiden's Latin school and registered at the university in 1620, though he probably never studied there. Six months spent in Amsterdam with Pieter Lastman around 1624 counted for far more than his formal apprenticeship: from Lastman came his taste for mythological and religious subjects, and his way of staging them with exaggerated gesture and vivid light.

He moved to Amsterdam for good in 1631 or 1632 and made his name almost immediately as the leading portraitist in the city. The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Tulp, painted in 1632, showed plainly what he could do that his rivals could not — it brought a vitality and richness to the group portrait that none of them had reached.

Gauguin, Paul.name: Paul Gauguin
Gauguin, Paul.places: Paris, Brittany, Tahiti and the Marquesas

context.text: He came to painting late and from an unlikely direction. He worked successfully as a stockbroker from 1872, painted as a keen amateur, collected Impressionists, and in 1883 gave up the job to paint full time. Success did not follow: he sold the collection to support his family, then left them behind for Brittany.

At Pont-Aven in 1888 he broke with Impressionism outright, laying down areas of flat, pure colour for expressive and symbolic ends. Colour was to be used unnaturalistically, for decoration or for feeling, and bounded by emphatic outlines that make rhythmic patterns like stained glass or a Japanese print. He was among the first Europeans to look for inspiration in ancient and non-European art.

He sailed for Tahiti in 1891, wanting out of everything artificial and conventional — after the disease of civilisation, he wrote, life there was a return to health. He painted his best pictures in the South Seas, in constant poverty and bad health, often unable to get proper materials and forced to spread his colours thin. He died in the Marquesas in 1903.

Neglected for centuries and now among the best-loved painters of the Renaissance. 'Botticelli' means 'little barrel' and was first a nickname for a portly older brother, before the family took it as a surname. He trained under Filippo Lippi, whose sweetness and grace stayed with him, but his own drawing is finer — an unusual combination of delicacy and flowing vitality.

He spent almost his whole life in Florence, his one significant journey being to Rome in 1481–2 to work on the Sistine Chapel. Through the 1480s he seems to have been the most sought-after painter in the city, working for the civic authorities, the major churches and above all the Medici. Primavera and the Birth of Venus were probably painted for the Medici patron who also commissioned his Dante drawings.

His fortunes fell away in the 1490s, and once Leonardo returned to Florence in 1500 his linear style must have looked archaic. He ended in financial trouble; Vasari describes him as old and useless, unable to stand upright and getting about on crutches. By the time he died he was a relic of an age that had passed.

He turned Venice from a city that was provincial in its painting into one that rivalled Florence and Rome, and he gave its art a character of its own — worked out through colour, light and atmosphere rather than through the line that preoccupied Florence. Nearly every Venetian painter of the following generation trained in his studio.

His career is poorly documented and few of his paintings can be securely dated, so his development can only be followed in broad outline. Over more than half a century he moved from a sharp linear manner with roots in the Middle Ages to something broad, mellow and classically dignified. The strongest influence on the early work was his brother-in-law Mantegna.

He never stopped taking things in. Antonello da Messina, in Venice in 1475–6, showed him oil painting and a lucid way with space and form; a picture from the year before his death is strongly marked by Giorgione, who was young enough to be his grandson. He borrowed constantly and still ended up sounding like nobody else.

One of the greatest of Caravaggio's followers, and a formidable person. She was painting remarkably well while still in her teens, built a reputation across Europe, and lived with an independence rare for a woman of her time — in 1616, aged twenty-three, she became the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia del Disegno.

Her father Orazio, himself a gifted follower of Caravaggio, almost certainly trained her, but her style is nothing like his: where he tends towards the lyrical and refined, she is powerful and dramatic. Judith and Holofernes was the subject she made her own.

At seventeen she was raped by the painter Agostino Tassi, and during his trial she was tortured to test whether her evidence was true. Her preference for bloodthirsty subjects is commonly read against that: the ferocity with which she painted a woman beheading a man has often been taken as a kind of revenge in pictures.

The greatest figure of Renaissance art in northern Europe. He was a goldsmith's son, trained in his father's trade, with goldsmiths for grandfathers on both sides — but from early on he had intellectual ambitions that reached well past the medieval craftsman's workshop. His godfather was Nuremberg's leading publisher, and his closest friend from childhood became a poet and scholar with the best private library in Germany.

He was the first artist to paint himself again and again across a lifetime rather than once or twice. The earliest is a silverpoint drawing made when he was thirteen; in the three finished painted self-portraits he presents himself as a beautifully dressed and immaculately groomed gentleman, or even as a Christ-like figure, rather than as a humble craftsman.

He learned woodcut from Michael Wolgemut, the leading painter in Nuremberg, then spent 1490 to 1494 travelling for experience. He went to Colmar in 1492 hoping to meet Schongauer, the most illustrious German engraver of the day, and arrived to find him recently dead; Schongauer's brothers gave him introductions that got him work illustrating books in Basle. A few months after an arranged and unhappy marriage he left his wife behind for a study visit to Venice.

He started as a pillar of the Viennese establishment, successful with lavish ornamental decorative schemes, and became a hero of the avant-garde within a few years. In 1897 he and a group of friends resigned from the conservative Viennese Artists' Association to set up the Sezession, and he was elected its president.

Scandal sealed the change. His enormous allegorical murals for Vienna University — Jurisprudence, Medicine and Philosophy — were denounced as nonsensical and pornographic; he abandoned the commission in 1905, and the paintings burned in 1945. Official work dried up after that, but private patrons kept coming, for portraits as well as mythological and allegorical subjects.

His figures are painted more or less naturalistically and then embellished, in their clothing or in the background, with dense decorative pattern recalling butterfly or peacock wings. The result is a lush sensuality nobody else quite reached. He mattered to Kokoschka and Schiele, but the manner was too personal to found a school.

His career is full of contradictions. He spent years obstinately making work that Paris would not have, criticised for its 'Gothic' distortions, and was surprised in 1824 to find himself acclaimed and installed as leader of the academic opposition to Delacroix and Romanticism — a position he then held for the rest of his life.

Line is the constant. His contours do more than contain and delineate a form; they have a sensuous beauty of their own, and that holds from the portraits of 1805 through to the Turkish Bath of 1863, painted when he was past eighty. He went on working with great energy into his eighties, and some of his best portraits come from those last years.

The deepest contradiction is in the work itself. He was held up as the guardian of classical rules and precepts, but what makes him a great painter is his personal obsessions and mannerisms. He lived like a bourgeois; his finest pictures come out of a deeply sensuous nature.

Renoir, Pierre-Auguste.name: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
Renoir, Pierre-Auguste.places: Paris and the south of France

context.text: Born into a poor family, he went to work at thirteen painting porcelain in a Paris factory. It gave him two things that lasted: the light, fresh colour that marks his Impressionist work, and a respect for good craftsmanship. His taste for light-hearted subjects came from studying the Rococo masters in the Louvre.

By 1862 he had saved enough to pay for tuition and entered Gleyre's studio, where he met Monet, Sisley and Bazille and formed the early nucleus of the Impressionist group. He and Monet were especially close then, and the pictures the two of them painted side by side at La Grenouillère in 1869 are taken as the classic early statements of the style.

He had a hard time of it early on, then found success as a portraitist in the late 1870s — a shy but friendly manner put sitters at their ease. From 1881 the dealer Durand-Ruel bought his work regularly and the money worries stopped. By then he felt he had gone as far as Impressionism could take him, and a visit to Italy sent him after greater solidity: The Umbrellas, begun before the trip and finished after it, has feathery Impressionist brushwork on the right and something crisper on the left.

He spent his whole known career in 's-Hertogenbosch and took his name from it; he was really Jerome van Aken. The town sat well away from the main Netherlandish art centres but was one of the most prosperous in Brabant, with a vigorous intellectual life. He came from a long line of artists, married a wealthy woman, and probably had no need to paint for a living.

Because the pictures look so strange now, they have attracted theories that he dabbled in heresy, witchcraft or the occult. The contemporary evidence points the other way: he held the orthodox religious views of his time and was a prominent member of a local religious brotherhood. The idea that he hid unorthodox beliefs in his work seems to have appeared only after his death, and the wilder speculation is a twentieth-century habit. Modern research reads the work as a reflection of the culture around him rather than as private eccentricity.

About forty paintings are accepted as his, none of them dated. More than half take traditional Christian subjects, and only a few are dominated by the nightmare imagery his name is now inseparable from. Much of that imagery can be explained by the popular culture he lived in — proverbs and devotional literature — and his monsters have relatives in the margins of medieval manuscripts and in Gothic gargoyles, including some on his own town's cathedral. His handling stands apart too: vigorous and varied, where the period preferred smooth and precise.

Working alongside Pissarro north of Paris in the early 1870s turned him around. Under that influence he took up landscape seriously, and studying nature closely moved him off the violent imaginary subjects of his youth and onto the real world in front of him. The gloomy tonality of the early work gave way to light and colour.

He showed at the first and third Impressionist exhibitions and was savaged both times, and he never wholly belonged to the group. He was after structural analysis rather than surface effects: the aim was to combine the formal grandeur of the Old Masters with the naturalism and colour of the best contemporary painting — to do Poussin again from nature, as he put it, and to make of Impressionism something solid and enduring, like the art of the museums.

He inherited the family estate in 1886 and spent his last twenty years doing almost nothing but paint: his wife, still lifes, and above all Provence and the Mont Sainte-Victoire. Where Monet wanted to finish a landscape in a single session and catch one moment, Cézanne returned to the same place again and again to build up an accumulated view — his pictures rarely say what time of day it is, or even the season. Depth and solidity come not from perspective and conventional drawing but from very delicate shifts of tone, with forms subtly tilted and stretched to reach the balance he wanted.

The greatest German Romantic painter, and one of the most original landscape painters there has been. He grew up near the Baltic in a strict Lutheran household, with a childhood marked by the deaths of his mother and three of his siblings, and he was intensely introspective and often melancholy. He worked from contemplation rather than from the motif: close your bodily eye, he wrote, so that you may see your picture first with your spiritual eye.

He began with topographical drawings and did not take up oils until 1807. One of the first, The Cross in the Mountains, caused an outcry because it was painted as an altarpiece — putting a landscape to that use struck some critics as sacrilege. His subjects broke new ground repeatedly: an infinite stretch of sea or mountains, plains under snow or fog in the strange light of sunrise, dusk or moonlight. Even where there is no overt religious symbol the landscapes carry a haunting spirituality.

When he puts people in, they are often seen from behind, so that being faceless they stand in for anyone. A severe stroke in 1835 sent him back to small sepias, and although he had real success earlier on, by the time he died he was virtually forgotten. His greatness was not widely recognised again until the end of the century, with the rise of Symbolism.

After Rubens, the outstanding Flemish painter of the seventeenth century, and known above all as one of the greatest portraitists there has been. He was exceptionally precocious: on his earliest dated painting, made at fourteen, he proudly inscribed his own age alongside the sitter's. From about 1617 he was Rubens's chief assistant while building a reputation of his own — by 1620 a visitor to Antwerp was reporting that his work was esteemed hardly less than his master's.

The early work leans on Rubens so heavily that experts still have trouble telling the two hands apart, though van Dyck is less energetic and more nervously sensitive — he was highly strung and slight where Rubens was robust. He copied his master's aristocratic way of living too: his manners, one contemporary wrote, were those of a lord rather than an ordinary man.

He went to Italy in 1621 and stayed six years, turning increasingly to portraiture with Titian as his model. Working mainly in Genoa he painted a series of grand pictures of the nobility that fixed a lasting aristocratic type: the slender figure and the proud bearing.

The greatest of the Neoclassical painters and one of the most influential European artists of his time. He won the Prix de Rome at his fifth attempt in 1774 and spent the years to 1780 in Italy, where he purged the Rococo out of his work and built a heroic style on antique sculpture, Poussin and Raphael.

What carried him to the front in Paris was not only the grandeur of the work but its moral seriousness, which suited the moment exactly. The Rococo was associated with the frivolity of court life, and as the royal family and the aristocracy grew unpopular his sternly Neoclassical pictures could be read as a demand for social as well as aesthetic change. The Oath of the Horatii of 1785 — three Roman brothers pledging their lives to the state — established him above everyone else.
He was entirely in sympathy with the Revolution of 1789. He served on its committees, voted for the execution of Louis XVI, designed its festivals, and turned his art directly into propaganda.

The outstanding Netherlandish painter of the mid-fifteenth century and one of the most influential artists in Europe — and yet almost nothing about his career is secure. Not one of the surviving paintings associated with him is signed, dated, or verified by indisputable contemporary documents.

The body of work has been assembled out of style instead. A few pictures can be identified from early sources, and the manner they share is distinctive enough that the rest has been gathered around them. The early years stay the murkiest part: a 'Rogelet de la Pasture' began an apprenticeship with Robert Campin in Tournai in 1427 and became a master there in 1432, and that is generally accepted to be him — though nobody can say why he would have started training so late.

The most celebrated painter of the Early Netherlandish school. Within a few years of his death he had a reputation on both sides of the Alps, and it has never faded — though he is no longer credited with having invented oil painting, as was long maintained.

From 1425 he served Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, for the rest of his life, as equerry as well as painter. Philip stood godfather to one of his children and sent him on diplomatic missions, including an embassy to Portugal in 1428–9 to arrange the duke's marriage. Only from 1432, when he settled in Bruges, does his career as an artist come into focus: every dated painting falls between 1432 and 1439.

His single portraits are all much alike in format — the sitter bust-length, in three-quarter view, against a plain background. They are more objective than Rogier van der Weyden's, the features put under relentlessly close scrutiny, and they still convey a sense of inner life. His technique became the accepted model for those who came after, although at home it was Rogier's more emotional manner that had the greater influence: the sheer perfection of van Eyck's work must have made him a daunting example to follow.

The son of a wealthy art-loving banker, trained first for the law, then taught by a pupil of Ingres who handed on that tradition of draughtsmanship. Most of his real education came from studying the Old Masters, in the Louvre and in Italy. Meeting Manet in 1862 — while copying a Velázquez — turned him away from history painting and towards the life around him.

He took part in seven of the eight Impressionist exhibitions but was Impressionist only in parts. He had little interest in landscape and so did not share the group's concern with changing light and atmosphere; even his racecourse pictures were painted in the studio with the setting left generalised. No other painter of the time drew on such a range of modern city subjects — the ballet and the theatre, café interiors, laundresses at work, women bathing.

The spontaneity is built, not caught. He liked unfamiliar viewpoints and figures cut off as if in a snapshot, and he was keenly interested in photography, but the pictures were carefully composed: even working from nature, he said, one has to compose — no art was ever less spontaneous than his. From about 1886 his eyesight was in serious trouble, and he turned from oils to pastel, which put him physically closer to the surface he was working on.

The leading artist in northern Italy for most of his career. He was the pupil and adopted son of Squarcione in Padua and grew up in a humanist atmosphere that coloured his whole approach to art — including, at about seventeen, taking his master to court and forcing him to recognise his independence.

The style he arrived at almost at once barely changed in essentials over the next half-century: sharp clarity of drawing, colour and lighting; a passion for archaeology fed by the classical remains all around him; and a command of perspective and foreshortening unequalled in the fifteenth century. For all the learning he is never dry — there is wit and fancy in the work, and he painted animals with obvious pleasure.

From 1460 he was court painter to the Gonzaga in Mantua and stayed in their service for life. His most famous work is the Camera degli Sposi in the Ducal Palace, where the family are arranged in courtly scenes below medallions of the Caesars, implying the house was fit to continue Rome. The remarkable part is the illusionistic architecture, above all the ceiling, which appears to extend the real space of the room — the first scheme of its kind since antiquity, and the foundation for centuries of painting in that vein.

He was the main creator of the High Renaissance style, cutting incidental detail back to reach a greater unity of form and atmosphere. Sfumato is his: tones and colours blended so subtly that they melt into one another with no perceptible transition — without lines or borders, in his own words, in the manner of smoke.

He worked too slowly for fresco, which has to be painted fast and cannot be reworked, so for the Last Supper he tried an experimental technique instead. It began to deteriorate almost immediately, and the picture has spent most of the five centuries of its fame in poor condition.

After he abandoned Milan in 1499 he moved about constantly — Venice, Mantua, two years as a military engineer for Cesare Borgia, back to Milan, then Rome — but the work of his later years centred on Florence. The Mona Lisa was begun there around 1503, its pose and expression natural and subtle enough to make most earlier portraits look rigid.

Norway's greatest artist, and his subjects came straight out of his own life. His mother and eldest sister died of consumption while he was young, and his grief-stricken father turned almost dementedly pious. Illness, madness and death, he wrote, were the black angels that kept watch over his cradle. Jealousy, sickness and the waking of sexual desire recur again and again in the work, and he painted extreme psychological states with a conviction nobody had managed before.

He began in a conventional naturalistic manner, then fell in with the bohemian artists and writers of Christiania who outraged respectable society by arguing for sexual as well as artistic freedom. Visits to Paris from 1885 brought him the Impressionists and the Symbolists, and above all Gauguin's simplified forms and unnaturalistic colour. In 1892 an exhibition of his work in Berlin caused such an uproar in the press that it was closed — which made him famous in Germany overnight, and he based himself there for the next sixteen years.

He is named after the small town in Emilia where he was born and died. He worked mainly in provincial centres and his reputation in his own lifetime was modest, yet he was one of the most sophisticated artists of his time, and his posthumous fame and influence were enormous.

His training has to be inferred from his style. Mantegna is the obvious source for the early work, and Mantua is near enough his home town that he may well have studied there, possibly even with the aged Mantegna himself. Later he absorbed more of Leonardo — the introspection, and the soft sfumato — which helped produce the fluid, elegant, alluring manner he is known for. His most characteristic pictures are altarpieces and small devotional works, often very tender and intimate.

A Florentine Mannerist and the pupil of Pontormo, who virtually adopted him as a son and put his portrait as a child into one of his own paintings. Bronzino remained deeply attached to him, and the early style is so close that pictures from around 1530 can be hard to assign to one hand or the other. But he lacked Pontormo's emotional intensity, his colouring and brushwork were harder, and he was a far better portraitist than religious painter.

From 1539 he worked for Duke Cosimo I de' Medici and spent most of the rest of his career in that service, becoming the leading painter in Florence and producing an unforgettable run of images of his patron's family and courtiers — immaculately polished pictures that carry the splendour and the formality of the world they lived in. He was a poet as well, and his most personal portraits are perhaps those of other literary figures.

One of the greatest figures in the history of landscape painting. He showed a talent for drawing early and earned money as a boy colouring prints; he exhibited a watercolour at the Royal Academy at fifteen and was made a full Academician at twenty-six, the second-youngest anyone had managed to that point. He called the topographical watercolourist Thomas Malton his real master.

He painted only in watercolour at first and did not exhibit an oil until 1796. The career prospered: he was hard-working, a good businessman and frugal by nature, though he lived rather squalidly. From early on he was conscious of his place in the tradition of landscape painting, and often made pictures in homage to his great predecessors, or in rivalry with them.

One of the most individual talents in British art. He set up as a portrait painter in Ipswich in 1752, working for the merchants of the town and the local squires — mostly heads and half-lengths, but also some small groups posed in a landscape. Moving to Bath in 1759 changed the clientele entirely, and from then on the portraits are life-size and often full-length, done in a free and elegant manner.

Portraiture was his profession, he said, but landscape painting was his pleasure. He went on painting landscapes long after he had left the countryside, sometimes building them up in the studio from twigs and pebbles arranged to stimulate his imagination. He was a founder member of the Royal Academy in 1768 — the only portraitist from outside London so honoured — and became a favourite of the royal family even though Reynolds held the official appointment.

The most celebrated of all painters of ideal landscape — famous enough that he is usually called simply Claude. He was born in Lorraine but spent almost his whole career in Rome, arriving before 1620 and reportedly working first as a pastry cook, a favourite trade of Lorrainers, before entering Agostino Tassi's household and rising from domestic servant to studio assistant.

Two years studying in Naples left him permanently marked by the beauty of the gulf, which recurs in his paintings for the rest of his life. By the early 1630s he was among the leading landscape painters in Rome and his work was already attracting imitators. To guard against forgeries he began keeping a record of his own pictures: the Liber Veritatis, an album started around 1635 that details virtually everything he painted.
A pupil and friend of Thomas Cole, he carried on the Hudson River School's appetite for spectacular natural scenery. His Niagara of 1857 made him the most famous painter in the United States.

He did not stay at home for his subjects. He travelled widely and painted the tropical forests of South America, icebergs and erupting volcanoes, often on an enormous scale. The work was immensely popular in his own day, went through a long period of neglect, and is now coming back into favour. His house, Olana, above the Hudson, is a museum.

The son of an outrageously eccentric nobleman, he grew up loving horses and sport; then an inherited illness and two falls in his early teens stopped the bones in his legs growing and left him permanently stunted. He was not the midget of popular imagination — about five feet, above the minimum height for military service — but his head looked disproportionately large and he walked with difficulty. He was stoical about it and never mentioned it except as a joke, and coming to terms with it left him with a hatred of pretence of any kind. That is what you see in the frankness of the pictures.

In January 1884, aged nineteen, he was given an allowance and set up a studio of his own in Montmartre, a district notorious for its bohemianism and its seedily glamorous nightlife. Almost everything he made comes out of that world: cafés, brothels and nightclubs.

Mondrian, Piet.name: Piet Mondrian
Mondrian, Piet.places: The Netherlands, Paris and New York

context.text: He did not start out abstract. The early paintings are naturalistic and direct, often delicate in colour; between 1907 and 1910 they turned Symbolist, partly under Toorop's influence and perhaps partly because he had taken up Theosophy. Cubism reached him between 1912 and 1914, and he painted a series on the theme of a tree in which the image grows steadily more fragmented. By 1914 he had virtually eliminated the curved line.

In 1917 he joined Theo van Doesburg in founding De Stijl, which promoted a rigorously geometrical abstraction, and he became its main exponent. He called his own version Neo-Plasticism and confined himself to straight lines and primary colours — an art of great clarity and discipline that he believed reflected the laws of the universe, showing the immutable realities behind the changing appearance of things.

The most famous Polish painter of his time. Apart from periods of study in Munich and Vienna he was based in Cracow for his whole career, and from 1873 he was director of the city's School of Fine Arts.
He specialised in enormous, colourful canvases of notable scenes from Polish history — the Battle of Grunwald above all. He painted portraits too.

He made his name in 1627 with a powerful Christ on the Cross painted for a Dominican monastery in Seville, and its success brought him to settle in the city two years later. Apart from a set of mythological and historical pictures for Philip IV, a few portraits and some masterly still lifes, he gave himself almost entirely to religious images.

His most characteristic pictures are single figures of monks and saints at prayer or in meditation, set against a plain background so that they stand out with massive physical presence. Simple in composition and direct in feeling, they made him an ideal interpreter of Counter-Reformation doctrine, combining an austere naturalism with mystical intensity.

His nickname means the little Parmesan, after the city he came from and mostly worked in. He was precociously gifted: by 1522 he was painting highly accomplished frescos in Parma, showing his admiration for Correggio, who was at work in the same church. The originality was there from the start, especially a love of unusual spatial effects — most memorably in the Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror of 1524, in which, Vasari said, he looks so beautiful that he seemed an angel rather than a man.

In Rome from 1524 his work grew grander and more graceful under Raphael and Michelangelo, but what stayed with him was a disturbing intensity built from elongated forms, disjointed space, chill lighting and a lascivious atmosphere. He left after the sack of Rome in 1527, returned to Parma in 1530, and was imprisoned in 1539 for failing to deliver a fresco commission he had contracted for.

A Spaniard who spent his whole known career in Italy, where they called him Lo Spagnoletto, the little Spaniard. He settled in Naples in 1616, then a Spanish possession and one of the main centres of the Caravaggesque style. He is often filed as a follower of Caravaggio, and the early work is markedly tenebrist, but it is far more individual than most — the paint handled vigorously, almost scratchily — and the later pictures are a long way from Caravaggio, rich in colour and soft in modelling.

His taste for bloody martyrdom has been overplayed. He did paint some powerful scenes of the kind, but the treatment is always dignified rather than merely gory, and he was capable of great tenderness. What runs through the work, religious and secular alike, is a feeling for individual humanity.

The most celebrated Russian painter of his day and a central figure in the country's cultural life. Earlier Russians had won renown in the West with classical and biblical subjects; Repin was the first to achieve European fame with specifically Russian ones — scenes from Russian history, pictures of peasant life, portraits of a host of celebrities, and contemporary subjects attacking political abuses and social ills.

A scholarship took him to Europe from 1873 to 1876, most of it spent in Paris, where he became a respected figure and returned several times. He had mixed feelings about the Impressionists, whose first exhibition fell in the middle of that stay: he admired their lively use of light and colour but thought the work lacked serious moral purpose. How much those moral values mattered to him is plain in his first great success, Barge Haulers on the Volga.

He gave up a promising university career teaching law to paint, partly under the impact of a French Impressionist exhibition in Moscow where one of Monet's Haystacks struck him hard. He moved to Munich in 1896, and became one of the most important figures in the arrival of abstract art — as a theorist quite as much as a painter.

From 1909 he worked in series called Improvisations, Compositions and Impressions, gradually eliminating representational content until he arrived at pure abstraction around 1912. The musical titles are not decoration: he was interested in the correspondence between colours and sounds, played cello and piano, and was a friend of Schoenberg, whose atonality he took as the equivalent of his own experiments. He said he grasped that colour and line could carry feeling on their own after returning to his studio one evening and failing to recognise a painting of his own lying on its side.

Chiefly celebrated as one of the greatest portraitists there has been. He trained in Augsburg with his father, one of the leading artists there, and had moved to Basle by 1515, where he designed for printers and became the leading painter in the city — portraits, altarpieces, murals and designs for stained glass. His best-known printed work, the Dance of Death series, was cut in the mid-1520s but not published until 1538, after which it ran into many editions.

In 1526 he went to England carrying an introduction from Erasmus to Sir Thomas More. The group portrait he painted of More's family is a landmark: no earlier artist had shown a group at full length in their own home. He prospered, but returned to Basle in 1528, probably because staying away much longer would have cost him his citizen's rights.

He was Flemish by birth — his parents left Antwerp after the Spanish captured it in 1585 — and had settled in Haarlem by 1591, where he spent the rest of a long life. He married twice, had at least ten children, and was in money trouble throughout; in his last years he was destitute, and the Haarlem authorities granted him a small annual stipend four years before he died. The popular image of him as a drunken wife-beater has no real foundation.

He was the first great artist of the seventeenth-century Dutch school and is reckoned among the most brilliant portraitists anywhere. Almost everything he made is a portrait, and the handful of pictures that are not still feel like one. Nothing he did before 1616 prepares you for the life-size group portrait of the officers of the St George militia company he painted that year — there is no real precedent for its vigour, in his own work or anyone else's. His greatest gift was catching a fleeting movement or expression, which is what makes the faces feel alive.

From the 1920s he held, with Picasso, the reputation of foremost painter of the age. He was a late starter, having abandoned a legal career to begin studying art in 1891, and he was neither as prolific nor as versatile as Picasso — but for sensitivity of line and beauty of colouring he stood unrivalled among his contemporaries.

1905 was the year everything turned. He showed at the Salon d'Automne alongside Derain, Vlaminck and Marquet in the exhibition that launched Fauvism, and he found his first important patrons in the expatriate American Steins. Until then he had struggled to earn a living; from then on he was free of money worries and could afford to travel, and his growing reputation filled the art school he ran in Paris from 1907.

Tour, Georges de La.name: Georges de La Tour
Tour, Georges de La.places: Lunéville, in the Duchy of Lorraine

context.text: He had a fairly successful career — Louis XIII, Cardinal Richelieu and the Duke of Lorraine all owned his paintings — and then his name sank into oblivion after his death. He was not rediscovered until the twentieth century, when he was hailed as the most inspired of Caravaggio's followers. Little of his life is recorded, beyond his being arrogant and unpopular with his neighbours.

Nobody knows how he came by Caravaggio's manner. He may have visited Italy early on, or picked it up second-hand through a local painter or the Utrecht school. He is associated above all with night scenes lit by a single candle, but his handling of light is subtler than others working that way, grander in conception and more sombre in mood. In the mature work he smoothed his figures towards geometric simplicity and a monumental stillness.

Famous for allegorical 'portraits' assembled out of objects — fruit and vegetables arranged into the form of a human face. He began conventionally enough, designing stained-glass windows for Milan Cathedral and working on frescos and tapestries for the cathedrals at Monza and Como, and nothing in that earlier work anticipates what came next.

From 1562 to 1587 he served three Habsburg emperors in turn, first in Vienna and then in Prague, and the bizarre heads were made for them: Rudolf II appears as Vertumnus, the Roman god of orchards, his face composed of fruit and flowers. The pictures were much imitated in his lifetime, then treated as mere curiosities for centuries, until the Surrealists revived an interest in visual punning.

A Venetian who stands somewhat apart from the central Venetian tradition. He was born in Venice and probably trained there, but he worked almost everywhere else — Treviso, central Italy, a dozen years in Bergamo, back to Venice, then restlessly around the towns of the Marches, ending as a partly blind lay brother at the monastery of Loreto. That rootless life reflects an anxious, difficult temperament, and the work is extremely uneven.

It draws on a wide range of sources, northern European as well as Italian, and combines them with an acute freshness of observation. He is best known now for portraits, which often carry a mood of psychological unrest, but he worked mainly as a religious painter, and his altarpieces could be strikingly original: the Recanati Annunciation is full of brilliant colour and odd poses, including a startled cat. His work was little regarded for centuries.

Italian, but virtually his whole career was spent in France. He laid the foundations of his style at home, studying the Renaissance masters — the linear grace of his work has him often described as a spiritual heir of Botticelli, and his reclining nudes continue a line running back through Titian to Giorgione. From Cézanne he learned simple dignity of composition and subtle handling of colour.

Meeting Brancusi in 1909 turned him to stonecarving, which occupied him until the war made materials impossible to get; he went back to painting then, and his best pictures come from the last five years of a short life. The range is narrow — nearly all of his two dozen surviving sculptures are heads, and most of the paintings are portraits or female nudes — but everything shares an extreme elongation, simplified form and a superb rhythmic vitality. The only one-man show he had in his lifetime, in 1917, was closed by the police over the filth on display.

The greatest and most versatile of all Dutch landscape painters. Nothing is known about his training, so it is generally assumed his father taught him — a painter as well as a frame maker and picture dealer — with his uncle Salomon van Ruysdael presumably playing some part too.

He was extremely precocious: his earliest known paintings date from 1646, when he was probably no more than eighteen, and already show a mature and distinctive personality. He was prolific as well — some seven hundred paintings are reasonably given to him — and his range ran from forests and grain fields to beaches, seascapes, watermills and windmills, winter scenes and Scandinavian torrents, the last painted without his ever having been to Scandinavia. He could get poetry out of a virtually featureless patch of dune.

He is particularly associated with Delft, though he only lived there about six years. Those years produced the pictures his reputation rests on: a small number of tranquil masterpieces that catch the well-being of a peaceful and prosperous country — a sunny yard, or light coming into the corner of a burgher's house.

There is a kinship of spirit with Vermeer, his great Delft contemporary, and he sometimes comes close to him in delicate observation of light and lucidity of composition, though never in beauty of brushwork. After he moved to Amsterdam in the early 1660s the quantity of his output was more remarkable than the quality.

The most famous Danish painter of his period. He studied at the Copenhagen Academy, then travelled Europe from 1875 to 1881, including two years in Paris, where open-air painting took hold of him — and with it a particular interest in complex effects of light, such as daylight and lamplight fusing in one picture.

From 1882 he spent much of his time at Skagen, a village on the Jutland coast, where he was a leading figure in a colony of artists. The pictures he painted there include poetic views of figures on the beach in the blue light of summer evenings. He was a successful portraitist as well. From 1900 his career was marred by mental illness.

His name comes from Verona, where he was born and trained; from about 1553 he was based in Venice, and he counts as a Venetian. With Tintoretto he was the dominant figure in Venetian painting in the generation after Titian, and he had many major commissions.

The two were sometimes in direct competition but generally worked for different markets, and seem to have got on well personally. Both were at their best on a large scale. Tintoretto concentrated on religious pictures, worked almost entirely in Venice and almost entirely in oils; Veronese took secular commissions too, and some of his finest work is fresco painted outside the city.

One of the towering figures of Romanticism, and one of the last major artists to give a large part of his career to mural painting in the heroic tradition. He is commonly regarded as the last great European painter able to use the whole humanist repertory with conviction and originality: antique myth and medieval history, Faust and Hamlet, tiger and odalisque all yielded images of equal power in his hands.

He was the son of a diplomat who was ambassador at The Hague when he was born, though it has been suggested that his natural father was Talleyrand, a friend of the family. His mother was the daughter of one of the most distinguished furniture makers of the day. He was well educated and grew up loving literature and music as well as art.

He began as a lithographer and then an illustrator, moving to New York in 1859 as his work for Harper's Weekly started to succeed. During the Civil War, Harper's sent him to the front several times as a correspondent, and he produced memorable images of it by concentrating not on combat but on life behind the lines.

The war also gave him the material for his first major work in oils, Prisoners from the Front, which carries the same vivid but dispassionate reportage as the illustrations. When he had selected the thing carefully, he said, he painted it exactly as it appeared. Shown to great acclaim in 1866, it established his reputation as a painter.

He worked in Seville almost all his life. He started out in a naturalistic, tenebrist manner under Zurbarán's influence, then made his reputation with a series of eleven paintings on the lives of Franciscan saints in 1645–6 — after which he displaced Zurbarán as the leading painter in the city and held that position unrivalled for the rest of his life.
