Most of his paintings take religious subjects, appealing strongly to popular piety and setting out the doctrines of the Counter-Reformation church — the Immaculate Conception above all, which was his favourite theme. The mature style is a long way from the early work: idealised figures and soft, melting handling.

He ranks with Turner as one of the two greatest figures in British landscape painting. Both brought a new freedom and inventiveness to the subject and each respected the other, but their temperaments and their careers could hardly have contrasted more: Turner was precocious and quickly won both critical and financial success, while Constable was slow to mature and struggled to make a name in England — he was better appreciated in France.

He was a prosperous corn merchant's son, trained for the family business, and his passion for art was strong enough that in 1799 his father reluctantly let him enrol at the Royal Academy Schools. He studied there until 1802, but learned most by copying the great landscape masters.

He takes his name from the small Franconian town where he was born, and very little is known of his life before he moved to Vienna in 1501 or 1502 to work for the humanist circles around the new university. The stay was brief — he left in 1504 — but some of his finest and most original work belongs to it, including portraits and religious pictures with a remarkable feeling for the beauty of landscape.

The best example of that manner is probably the Rest on the Flight into Egypt, which sets the Holy Family in a glade of German pine forest. He painted it in 1504, just before moving to Wittenberg as court painter to Frederick the Wise, Elector of Saxony, where he stayed until 1550.

An American who spent most of her career in France and did very well out of it — she came from a prosperous family but made a good deal of money from her work as well. She settled in Paris in 1874 and became particularly friendly with Degas, who invited her to exhibit with the Impressionists; she showed in four of their eight group exhibitions.

She specialised in scenes of everyday life, her favourite subject being a mother with her child, though she never married. Her work was thoroughly Impressionist in the 1880s; from about 1890 the forms grew more solid and firmly outlined. She was an outstanding pastellist and printmaker. Comparing her with Berthe Morisot, the other leading woman of the group, Gauguin said Miss Cassatt had as much charm but more strength.

The most famous artist Sicily produced, and one of the major pioneers of oil painting in Italy. Vasari says he learned the technique from Jan van Eyck, but there is no evidence he ever went to northern Europe and he was probably still a boy when van Eyck died. More likely he picked up northern methods in Naples, then dominated artistically by the Netherlands, where an early source has him studying under the leading Neapolitan painter of the day.

His life is poorly documented and his only certain visit to the Italian mainland was in 1475–6, when he was in Venice. He painted a large altarpiece there for the church of S. Cassiano, of which only three fragments survive.

One of the prime movers of Romanticism and among its most original figures. He studied in Paris but learned more by copying the Old Masters in the Louvre, developing a particular passion for Rubens. His first Salon submission, in 1812, won a gold medal — a dashing battle scene celebrating French military prowess at the height of Napoleon's power.

He failed to win the Prix de Rome but went to Italy anyway in 1816, his family being wealthy enough for him to travel and study at leisure. Back in Paris he began his masterpiece, the Raft of the Medusa, which caused a sensation at the Salon of 1819: some critics admired it and it was awarded a medal, but a great many viewers found it outrageous. He was dead at thirty-two.

The outstanding American landscape painter of the first half of the nineteenth century and a founder of the Hudson River School. His family emigrated from Lancashire in 1818 and he became passionately attached to the scenery of his new country. He was an immediate success in New York, and soon began making sketching trips up the Hudson valley; he settled there, at Catskill, in 1836.

A visit to Europe in 1829–32 changed his direction. Partly under the influence of Turner and John Martin he turned from natural scenery towards grandiose historical and allegorical themes, in two great series of paintings: The Course of Empire and The Voyage of Life.

He was born into a prosperous and cultured farming family in Normandy and trained in Paris. His early work was portraits, then small mythological and pastoral scenes; with The Winnower, shown at the Salon of 1848, he turned to the pictures of rustic life his name is now inseparable from.

The timing was exact. King Louis Philippe had been deposed earlier that same year, which created an appetite for pictures of ordinary people — The Winnower was bought by a minister in the new republican government. Critics read him through their own politics: republicans took him to be showing the dignity of the labouring poor.

An American who worked mainly in England, and an inveterate traveller — he spent part of his childhood in Russia, where his father had gone to work as a civil engineer. His training began sideways: discharged from West Point for deficiency in chemistry, he learned etching as a cartographer for the US navy.

He moved to Paris in 1855, studied intermittently under Gleyre, copied in the Louvre, and picked up two lasting enthusiasms: an admiration for Velázquez, and a devotion to the cult of the Japanese print and oriental decoration generally.

Rembrandt's most gifted pupil, and a painter of outstanding originality — but he died at thirty-two when the Delft gunpowder magazine exploded and devastated the town. Only a tiny body of his work survives, and much of it may have perished in the same disaster.

Only about a dozen paintings by him are known and they show great variety. The earliest are strongly marked by Rembrandt, but he broke free of his master and worked out a personal style with an exquisite feeling for cool colour harmonies, even when painting on a small scale.

He spent almost all his career in New York, though he travelled extensively around the United States, making long journeys by car. He trained at the New York School of Art under Robert Henri, and made three trips to Europe, mainly Paris, between 1906 and 1910.

He trained in Bologna, transferring to the academy the Carracci ran, where he absorbed their tradition of clear, firm draughtsmanship. He was based in Rome from 1601 to 1614. A brief flirtation with the Caravaggesque manner aside, Raphael and the antique were the sources of his graceful classical style.

His most celebrated work is the ceiling fresco Aurora, painted in 1614 for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, whose uncle Pope Paul V also favoured him. Despite that success in Rome he settled back in Bologna the same year and seldom left the city again.

He and his brother and cousin were major figures in the move from Mannerism to the Baroque, and largely responsible for making Bologna — until then something of an artistic backwater — the centre of the most distinctive tradition in seventeenth-century Italian painting. Reacting against the artificiality of Mannerism, they revived the solidity and grandeur of the High Renaissance and added a vigour and warmth that came from their admiration for Venetian painting.

The three often worked together early on, and it is not easy to tell their individual shares apart in the fresco cycles they painted jointly in Bologna. In the early 1580s they opened a private academy in the cousin's studio, and it quickly became a centre for progressive art.

He was brought up as an unwanted child in a Carmelite friary in Florence and took his vows there in 1421, but he was a reluctant friar. He had a scandalous affair with a nun, Lucrezia Buti, who bore him a son — the painter Filippino Lippi — and a daughter. The couple were released from their vows and allowed to marry, though he went on signing himself 'Frater Philippus'.

Vasari's account of his life, romantically embroidered to include capture by Moorish pirates, is one of the most colourful in the Lives, and it produced the lasting picture of a worldly Renaissance artist in revolt against the discipline of the Church. His life was certainly more eventful than most, but there is little solid evidence about his character.

With Mondrian, the most important pioneer of geometric abstract art. He started out in an unexceptional Post-Impressionist manner; by 1912 he was painting peasant subjects in a massive tubular style, and pictures combining the fragmented form of Cubism with the multiplied image of Futurism.

Representation dissatisfied him: he wanted, as he put it, to free art from the burden of the object. He was deeply religious with mystical leanings, and believed that giving up the external world would let him break through to a deeper level of meaning — to swim, in his phrase, in the white free abyss. He reached for the analogy of flight and space often when talking about his paintings.

The most energetic member of the Futurists and the only major sculptor among them. He signed both manifestos of Futurist painting in 1910 and wrote the one on sculpture in 1912. Advocating a complete break with the art of the past, he was centrally occupied with the movement's two preoccupations: making work that was emotionally expressive, and representing time and movement.

The early Futurist pictures often take up social themes, big city life especially. After a visit to Paris in 1912 brought him under the influence of Cubism, he tended to use his paintings as vehicles for his theories rather than as comments on the life around him, and that eventually carried him close to abstraction.

The most famous painter of the Sienese school, and very little is known about him. He is first recorded in 1278, records survive of several commissions, and he was fined on a number of occasions for minor offences — one of them perhaps involving sorcery.
Only one fully documented work by him survives: the Maestà commissioned by Siena Cathedral and finished in 1311.

He was born in the Virgin Islands, where his French-Jewish father and Creole mother ran a prosperous general store, was schooled in Paris, went back to the Caribbean, and did not settle in France until 1855. He met Monet in 1859 and became a central figure of Impressionism — the only artist to take part in all eight of the group's exhibitions.

About a decade older than most of the others, he was a much-respected father figure to them, and his gift for teaching gave him influence even over artists of greater stature: both Cézanne and Gauguin spoke glowingly of him. Being a guide and a mediator has perhaps obscured how good a painter he was in his own right. He introduced Cézanne to painting out of doors at Pontoise in 1872, experimented with Neo-Impressionism for several years after meeting Seurat in 1885, then returned around 1890 to his Impressionist manner with a freer touch than before.

The founder of Neo-Impressionism and much its greatest exponent. His parents were comfortably off, so he never had to worry about earning a living and could pursue his researches with single-minded dedication. After military service interrupted his studies he spent two years doing almost nothing but draw — broad velvety areas of tone in conté crayon on textured paper — which made him one of the subtlest draughtsmen of the century.

For all that mastery of black and white, as a painter he looked to the colourists, Delacroix and the Impressionists, and read scientific and aesthetic treatises alongside. The theory was that colours set side by side and mixed in the eye would be more luminous than the same colours mixed on the palette. Bathers at Asnières was still experimental; Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, shown at the last Impressionist exhibition in 1886, states the idea in full. He was dead at thirty-one.

His nickname comes from his father's trade of cloth dyer. He ranks second only to Titian among the Venetian painters of his time, and where Titian's late work went mostly to foreign patrons, Tintoretto worked for Venetians — above all supplying religious pictures to the city's churches and charitable institutions. He is recorded outside Venice only once in his life, and most of his work is still in the buildings it was painted for.

Little is known about his character and his career before about thirty is poorly documented. His greatest works are the vast series painted between 1564 and 1587 for the Scuola di S. Rocco, the wealthiest of the Venetian charitable confraternities.

One of the most powerful personalities in nineteenth-century art, and a prosperous farmer's son from the foot of the Jura. The country upbringing stayed with him: he spent most of his career in Paris but rarely painted urban subjects — his palette smells of hay, Cézanne said of him. He was obstinately self-assured and claimed to be self-taught; in fact he studied with various minor masters, though he learned more from copying Caravaggio and Velázquez in the Louvre, which is where the solid, weighty style and the strong contrasts of light and shade come from.

Politics caught up with him. After the Commune he was given six months' imprisonment for his part in pulling down the Vendôme Column, and on release was held personally liable for the cost of putting it back up. Unable to pay and fearing arrest, he went into exile in Switzerland and spent his last four years there, painting mainly landscapes and portraits.

German by birth but active in Bruges from 1465, and nothing of the German background shows in the paintings, which are closely connected to Rogier van der Weyden — by plausible tradition his teacher. His softened, sweetened version of Rogier's manner made him the most popular Netherlandish painter of his day: where Rogier excelled at intense emotion, Memling's impeccably crafted pictures are quiet, restrained, pious and beautifully balanced.

Tax records show he was one of the wealthiest citizens of Bruges, and his large output means he must have run a busy workshop. His style changed very little, which makes undated paintings hard to place in sequence. He showed rather more originality in portraiture than in religious work.

Most critics regard him as the outstanding American painter of the nineteenth century and many as the greatest his country has produced. He spent almost his whole career in Philadelphia; his one substantial absence was four years in Europe, training in Paris but learning more from six months in Spain, where the unaffected naturalism and sombre dignity of Velázquez hit him hard.
He began teaching at the Pennsylvania Academy in 1876 and caused controversy with his radical ideas, particularly his insistence that study be based on nude models rather than plaster casts.

A child prodigy who was hard-working as well as gifted: he became the youngest student ever admitted to the Royal Academy Schools, at eleven. In 1848, with Rossetti and Holman Hunt, he founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood and took his share of the abuse thrown at them until Ruskin stepped in as their champion — and in 1855 he married Ruskin's former wife, after that first marriage had been annulled.

In the 1850s he moved away from the brilliantly coloured, minutely detailed Pre-Raphaelite manner towards something broader and more fluent: with a family to support, he said, he could not afford to spend a whole day on an area no larger than a five shilling piece. The subjects softened too, from morally uplifting themes towards sentiment and a good story, and he became enormously popular.

The most celebrated of naive artists. His nickname, Le Douanier, refers to a job with the Paris municipal toll service, though he never actually reached the rank of customs officer. He took up painting as a self-taught hobby at about forty, exhibited regularly from 1886, and retired early in 1893 to give himself to it. He was extraordinarily ingenuous and suffered a great deal of ridicule — sometimes taking sarcastic remarks literally and reading them as praise — as well as real poverty, and his faith in his own ability never wavered.

He was trying to paint in the academic manner of the traditionalists, and what came out instead won him the admiration of the avant-garde. Vollard and his circle 'discovered' him around 1906, and in 1908 Picasso threw a banquet in his honour, half serious and half burlesque. He is best known now for the jungle scenes, from Tiger in a Tropical Storm to The Dream, painted the year he died.

A pupil of Delaroche, he inherited a highly finished academic style and had a career of great public success with it. For variety and sensationalism of subject he outdid every rival at the Salon — murder in the Roman senate, carnage in the arena, nudity at the slave auction and the harem bath, Bonaparte before the Sphinx — all plotted as carefully staged picture-plays, graced with sex, spiced with gore, and polished to a waxwork lifelikeness that his admirers took for realism.
He carried considerable influence as an upholder of academic tradition and an enemy of progressive trends, opposing the acceptance of the new painting at every turn.

Francesca, Piero della.places: Borgo San Sepolcro, Arezzo and Urbino

context.text: Virtually forgotten for centuries after his death, and now regarded as one of the supreme artists of the Renaissance. He spent much of his life in his native Borgo San Sepolcro and was clearly attached to it — he twice served as a town councillor, and the countryside around it turns up in the backgrounds of his paintings. His career is scantily documented and his movements cannot be followed in detail.

He was a habitually slow worker, which made ordinary fresco — a technique demanding speed and a sure hand — a poor fit. He experimented with ways round it, sometimes laying wet cloths on the plaster overnight so that, against normal practice, he could keep working on the same patch for more than a day.

A key figure in the second phase of Pre-Raphaelitism. He went to Oxford in 1853 meaning to train for the priesthood; William Morris, his fellow student, turned his interest to art, and then Rossetti, who remained the decisive influence. He left without a degree in 1856. Rossetti gave him a few informal lessons and he attended life classes for a while, but essentially he taught himself, and his taste ran more classical than his mentor's — the elongated forms owe a great deal to Botticelli.

He favoured medieval and Arthurian subjects and detested the modernists, dismissing the Impressionists' subject matter as landscape and whores. His reputation crumbled after his death and did not seriously revive until the 1960s.

One of the early Impressionist group. He entered Gleyre's studio in Paris in 1862 and met Monet, Renoir and Sisley there, painting out of doors with them at Fontainebleau and in Normandy. He was a figure painter rather than a landscapist, though he sometimes set his compositions in the open air. He came from a wealthy family and gave Monet and Renoir generous financial support. He was killed in action in the Franco-Prussian War at twenty-eight, cutting short a promising career.

His life is poorly documented and nobody knows who trained him, though Gentile Bellini is generally agreed to be the main influence. His reputation rests on two great cycles of paintings: scenes from the life of St Ursula, made in the 1490s, and a second cycle mainly on St George and St Jerome, painted in 1502–7 and still in the building it was made for.

His salient qualities — a taste for anecdote and an eye for the crowded detail of the Venetian scene — found their happiest expression in those cycles, and one of them looks forward to Canaletto and Guardi two centuries later. He had little flair for the altarpieces that filled his later years, but he was an excellent portraitist.

One of the greatest and most individual Netherlandish painters of his period, and nothing is known of his life before 1467, when he became a master in the Ghent painters' guild. Ghent gave him a good deal of temporary work — processional banners and the like — and by 1475 he was dean of the guild. Around the same time he entered a monastery near Brussels as a lay brother, though he went on painting and travelling.

He had a tendency to acute depression, and in 1481 he suffered a mental breakdown. He recovered, but died the following year. An account of the illness survives, written by a monk at the monastery who was evidently jealous of him.

The dominant figure in Die Brücke. Like the rest of the group he took from Post-Impressionism — Gauguin and van Gogh above all — as well as from Fauvism and Munch. He claimed to have been the first of them to appreciate Polynesian and other non-European art, which he saw in a Dresden museum, though it had little visible effect on his work.

He painted mainly figure compositions, portraits and nudes, often spending summers in seclusion in the country or on the coast where he could draw models moving naturally. The forms are harsh, and there is frequently an explicit eroticism and sometimes a feeling of malevolence.

He came from a family wealthy enough that he built and raced yachts as a hobby, and for many years after his death he was remembered mainly for the financial help he gave the Impressionists — buying their paintings, and sometimes simply giving them money. Since the 1960s his own work has been reassessed and he is now reckoned an artist of considerable if uneven achievement.

He showed at five of the eight Impressionist exhibitions, concentrating on scenes of everyday life. The most striking thing about the pictures is his appetite for unusual viewpoints and bold perspective effects.

Co-founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848, and the only member who stayed faithful to its aims for his whole career. He summarised those aims as finding serious and genuine ideas to express, studying nature directly in disregard of arbitrary rules, and picturing events as they must actually have happened rather than as convention had them.

The work is remarkable for its minute precision, its accumulation of incident, and its didactic insistence on moral or social symbolism. His devotion to authenticity was close to fanatical: he made three journeys to the Middle East so that he could paint biblical scenes with accurate local detail.
He spent almost his whole career in Italy, and is regarded not only as the greatest French painter of the seventeenth century but as the mainspring of the classical tradition in French painting.

His interest in art found direction when a mediocre late Mannerist painter came to his home town in Normandy on a church commission. He moved to Paris soon after and probably stayed until leaving for Rome in 1623, though those years are poorly documented and he may have travelled around France a good deal.

The leading artist in Bruges in the generation after Jan van Eyck's death in 1441. He was traditionally taken for van Eyck's pupil, and has even been credited with finishing works the master left incomplete, but it now seems likelier that he trained elsewhere before arriving. He was strongly influenced by van Eyck all the same, and helped spread his manner.

His own work is plainer and more summary, and his figures tend towards the doll-like. Rogier van der Weyden shows through in places too — his Lamentation is clearly built on Rogier's Descent from the Cross.

The outstanding artist in Haarlem of his day, and almost nothing is known about him. An early biographer says he was a pupil of Ouwater and died at about twenty-eight. His name means 'Little Gerard of the Brethren of St John', after the Haarlem order he was a lay brother of.

His one documented work is a Crucifixion triptych painted for the Brethren's church, of which two large panels survive. Their slender, doll-like figures with smooth, rather egg-like heads are distinctive enough that a body of about fifteen paintings has been gathered around them.

One of the outstanding artists of his generation in and around Florence. Vasari has him studying in turn with Leonardo, Albertinelli, Piero di Cosimo and Andrea del Sarto, whose workshop he entered in 1512; Andrea certainly marked the early work.

He was precocious — Michelangelo praised him while he was still a youth — and by about 1518 he had a style of his own, full of restless movement and disconcertingly irrational effects of scale and space, which put him at the front of Mannerism. That emotional tension reaches its height in his Entombment.

His nickname comes from Perugia, where he mainly worked. The early career is obscure, but he seems to have formed his style in Florence, where Vasari has him studying with Verrocchio at about the time Leonardo was training there too.
By 1481 he was well enough known to be commissioned, alongside Botticelli and others, to paint frescos on the walls of the newly built Sistine Chapel for Pope Sixtus IV.

His early work was academic; visits to Paris in 1903 and 1907 brought him Impressionism and Post-Impressionism, and van Gogh in particular pushed him towards Expressionism. In 1910 he met August Macke, who became his closest friend, and Kandinsky; with them he was a leading member of the Blaue Reiter, founded in 1911.

He was deeply religious and troubled by a profound spiritual malaise, and painted to uncover the mystical inner forces animating nature. The idea comes through most intensely in his pictures of animals, which he believed were both more beautiful and less corrupted than people. He was killed at Verdun at thirty-six.

His work represents better than anyone's the frivolity and elegant superficiality of French court life in the middle of the eighteenth century. His father was a minor painter, and probably gave him his first lessons.

He had a disturbed adolescence with certain affinities to Munch's, and it seems to have disposed him similarly towards angst-ridden and sexually charged imagery: his father died mad when he was fifteen, he disliked his mother, and he had a strange, possibly incestuous relationship with his younger sister, who often posed nude for him.

He studied at the Vienna Academy and met Klimt in 1907, who encouraged him and shaped his early Art Nouveau manner. By 1909 he had his own style: an aggressive linear energy carrying an acute nervous intensity. He painted portraits, landscapes and semi-allegorical subjects, but is best known for the drawings of nudes. He was dead at twenty-eight.

Bierstadt, Albert.name: Albert Bierstadt
Bierstadt, Albert.places: New York and the American West

context.text: German-born and active mainly in New York, he made several trips to the Far West and led the Rocky Mountain School, specialising in grandiose pictures of awesome mountain scenery. The paintings, often enormous, were immensely popular in his lifetime; his on-the-spot sketches are generally found more appealing now.

The greatest Italian painter of the eighteenth century and arguably the greatest European one, his work bringing the Italian tradition of fresco decoration — begun by Giotto four hundred years earlier — to a glorious conclusion. His output was prodigious and his career is essentially a story of ceaseless work; his services were sought from Spain to Sweden.

He trained with a history painter whose diligent manner he soon left behind, being, as a contemporary put it, all fire and spirit. He was influenced at first by Piazzetta's sombre drama and worked mainly in oils; from the mid-1720s he turned increasingly to fresco.

His scenes of frivolity and gallantry are among the fullest embodiments of the Rococo spirit — he has been called the fragrant essence of the eighteenth century. A brief spell with Chardin suited him badly; he then became Boucher's most brilliant pupil, and won the Prix de Rome in 1752 although he was not officially eligible, not being a student of the Académie Royale. It does not matter, Boucher said: you are my pupil.
He lived in Rome from 1756 to 1761 and there avoided the approved masters of the High Renaissance, finding his inspiration instead in a freer and more colourful tradition, Tiepolo above all.

The most famous view-painter of the eighteenth century. He began assisting his father, a theatrical scene painter, on sets for Vivaldi operas in Venice and Scarlatti operas in Rome. While in Rome he drew the ancient monuments and the famous modern buildings, and on returning to Venice he gave up theatrical work for topographical painting.

He came from a remarkable family: his father an exiled Italian patriot and Dante scholar, his sister the poet Christina Rossetti, his brother the critic William Michael. Growing up in modest circumstances but a strongly literary household, he found it hard at first to decide between poetry and painting.

Painting won, on the advice of the poet Leigh Hunt — if you paint as well as you write, you may be a rich man — but he went on writing verse and translating from the Italian, and has a secure place in literary history as well. In 1848 he founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood.

A central figure of the Impressionist group. Fragonard was her great-grandfather and she grew up in a highly cultured household; her training included some informal tuition from Corot. She had two pictures accepted by the Salon at her first attempt in 1864 and showed there for several years to encouraging reviews.

Progressive ideas drew her away, particularly after she met Manet in 1868 — she married his brother in 1874 — and she submitted to the Salon for the last time in 1873. She became instead one of the mainstays of the Impressionist exhibitions, helping organise them and showing in seven of the eight.

Chiefly famous as the outstanding society portraitist of his age — Rodin called him the van Dyck of our times. His parents were prosperous, cultured Americans who had settled in Europe, and both his upbringing and his career were thoroughly international: he was once described as an American born in Italy, educated in France, who looks like a German, speaks like an Englishman and paints like a Spaniard.
The Spanishness of that description points at his deep admiration for Velázquez.

The greatest American painter of the eighteenth century. He was the stepson of an engraver, from whose large collection of prints he picked up a considerable knowledge of European art, but as a painter he was virtually self-taught. He set up his own practice in Boston while still in his teens, and by his early twenties was painting portraits whose sense of life and character completely outstripped anything colonial portraiture had produced.
Success did not settle him. He was diffident and self-doubting by nature, and came to see himself as a provincial figure cut off from the great European tradition.

With Copley the outstanding American portraitist of his period, and regarded as the creator of a distinctively American kind of portraiture. Much of his early career was spent in Scotland, England and Ireland; he settled permanently in America in 1793 and finally in Boston in 1805.

He quickly established himself as the best portraitist in the country and painted many of the notables of the new republic. His portraits of George Washington are the most famous of his works — he created three types, all endlessly copied.

He always signed himself a Venetian, but he is recorded in the city only once — in 1457, when he was fined and given six months' imprisonment for adultery — and spent most of his career in the Marches. In 1490 he was knighted by the Prince of Capua, which says something about the reputation he enjoyed at the time.
His paintings are all religious, done in an elaborate and deliberately old-fashioned style that owes a good deal to the wiry Paduan tradition.

The son and pupil of Filippo Lippi, who died when the boy was about twelve. 'Little Filippo' then studied with Botticelli and learned a great deal from his expressive line, though his own manner, while sensitive and poetic, is more robust than his master's.

His first major commission, around 1485, was to finish Masaccio's fresco cycle in the Brancacci Chapel — a job he carried out with such skill and tact that it is sometimes hard to see where his work begins and where painting from more than half a century earlier ends.

One of the leading Symbolists. He was a close friend of Théodore Chassériau and took from his exotic Romanticism, but went far past him in a feeling for the bizarre, arriving at a manner highly distinctive in both subject and technique. The pictures are typically mystical and intense.

A pioneer of landscape as a subject in its own right. His paintings nominally take religious subjects, but the figures are often dwarfed by the world around them, and he is commonly described as the first landscape specialist in European art — the first painter to make his landscapes matter more than his figures.

Nothing is known of his early life, but he probably came from the craggy gorge of the Meuse around Dinant. That scenery is nothing like the flat countryside of most of the Netherlands, and it no doubt lies behind the rocky backgrounds of his pictures.

Best known for humorous genre scenes — warm-hearted, animated pictures that treat life as a vast comedy of manners. In Holland he ranks next after Rembrandt, Vermeer and Hals in popularity, and 'a Jan Steen household' has entered the Dutch language for the kind of lively, untidy home so many of his paintings show.

An early biographer wrote that his paintings are like his way of life and his way of life like his paintings, and dwelt on the buffoonery. That is a one-sided view: he was a Catholic who also painted portraits and historical, mythological and religious subjects.

A pupil of Cosimo Rosselli, whose Christian name he took as a patronym. Nothing by him is signed, documented or dated, so the body of work rests on Vasari's account — one of the most entertaining lives in the book, portraying him as a highly eccentric loner who lived on hard-boiled eggs, cooking fifty at a time while he was boiling glue, to save fuel.

The paintings he is best known for are correspondingly idiosyncratic: fanciful mythological inventions populated by fauns, centaurs and primitive men, sometimes with a spirit of low comedy about them.

He spent his whole career in Leiden, where in 1628 he became the young Rembrandt's first pupil. The early work follows his master closely; after Rembrandt left for Amsterdam he worked out a manner of his own, built on minute detail and a surface of almost enamelled smoothness. He had first trained in his father's trade of glass engraving, which must have helped instil the taste for glossy surfaces.
He was astonishingly fastidious about his tools and his working conditions.

He and his brother Antonio ran a flourishing workshop together, first in Florence and from about 1484 in Rome. The surname means 'poulterer', evidently after their father's trade. Both are recorded as painters and sculptors, and disentangling their individual shares is difficult — but Antonio was the dominant figure and principally a goldsmith and bronze worker, while Piero was mainly a painter.

His style was formed by a long stay in Italy, and on returning to Utrecht in 1620 he became, with Baburen and Terbrugghen, one of the leading followers of Caravaggio in the Netherlands. The candlelight effects of his early pictures earned him the nickname Gherardo delle Notti, Gerard of the Night Scenes.
In the late 1620s he dropped the Caravaggesque manner for something lighter, and with it achieved an international reputation.

He trained with his parents, both miniaturists, and then with Jacques-Louis David. He revered David and became one of his favourite pupils, but he had a passionate nature and was drawn more to the colour and vibrancy of Rubens and the Venetians than to his master's Neoclassical severity.

He worked in Italy from 1793 to 1800, met Napoleon there, and was commissioned to paint portraits documenting his campaigns. Back in Paris he carried on in that vein with huge canvases like the Battle of Eylau, among the most stirring images of the Napoleonic era.

He won the Prix de Rome in 1850, and after returning to France in 1854 became an immensely successful and influential exponent of academic art — upholding traditional values, and contriving to keep avant-garde work out of the Salon.

The greatest French painter of his period and one of the key figures of the Rococo. Valenciennes had passed from the Spanish Netherlands to France only six years before he was born, and contemporaries regarded him as a Flemish painter; the links with Flanders are real enough, but the sophistication of the work is quintessentially French.

He moved to Paris around 1702 and spent about four years as pupil and assistant to Gillot, who gave him his interest in scenes from the theatre and from daily life. He then worked a year or two for Claude Audran, a leading decorative painter who was also a curator.

He took over his dead father's lithographic business in 1832 and was extremely industrious, making his name with four hundred illustrations for a history of Frederick the Great. He worked the same themes in painting with comparable success, and effectively created the popular image of the founder of the Prussian state.
From the 1860s he turned to modern life, and was among the first German painters to find picturesque qualities in industry.

Dutch-born, he settled in London in 1870 and took British citizenship three years later. He specialised in historical genre, starting with medieval subjects and turning to the ancient world after a visit to Pompeii in 1863.

The paintings conjure something close to a Hollywood vision of Greece and Rome — beautiful women, exotic costume, marbled settings — and were enormously successful. Punch called him a marbellous artist. He lived sumptuously in St John's Wood, in a house previously owned by Tissot which he remodelled as a Roman villa.

His style was solid, prosaic and rather old-fashioned, particularly set beside his great contemporary Botticelli — but he was an excellent craftsman and a good businessman, and ran one of the most prosperous workshops in Florence, helped by his younger brother Davide.
His largest undertaking was the fresco cycle in the choir of S. Maria Novella, illustrating scenes from the lives of the Virgin and St John the Baptist.

His nickname means 'the little Pisan', though he spent his early years in Verona and kept up the connection for most of his life. A successful career took him to Rome, Naples and several courts of northern Italy, particularly the Este at Ferrara and the Gonzaga at Mantua.

With Gentile da Fabriano he is regarded as the foremost exponent of International Gothic in Italian painting, but most of his major works have perished — including frescos in the Doges' Palace in Venice and in St John Lateran in Rome.

His nickname means 'the angelic brother', and popular tradition has taken him for not an artist properly so called but an inspired saint. He was in fact a highly professional painter, in touch with the most advanced developments in Florentine art, who travelled extensively in later life for prestigious commissions.
He is first recorded as a painter in 1417 and by 1423 had joined the Dominican Order at Fiesole, taking the name Fra Giovanni. He probably began as a manuscript illuminator.

The greatest of Dürer's contemporaries — and even his name is not his. He was really Mathis Gothardt or Neithardt, which was not discovered until the 1930s, and the origin of the nickname Grünewald, 'greenwood', is unknown; it seems not to have been used before the seventeenth century.

That haziness about his identity reflects both the isolation of his work and the obscurity he fell into after his death. He had no known pupils, and unlike most German artists of his time he made no woodcuts or engravings — which would have carried his name.

He worked in various cities of central Italy — Arezzo, Florence, Orvieto, Perugia and Rome — as well as his native Cortona. Vasari, who was related to him, records meeting him as a child of eight and calls him 'this good old man'.

The son of the composer Alexander Serov, he studied privately under Repin from an early age and then at the St Petersburg Academy. He painted landscapes, genre and historical subjects and illustrated books, but he is best known as a portraitist, and in that field he was the greatest Russian painter of his time and a match for anyone in the world.
Like his contemporary Sargent he was a cosmopolitan figure, at ease in high society, and he brought to the work something of the same aristocratic authority and poise.

Venetian by training — Vasari has him studying with Giovanni Bellini — but active mainly in Rome. His early work owes most to Giorgione, whose Three Philosophers he is said to have finished after the master died in 1510.
Their styles can be close enough that pictures are disputed between them, most notably the unfinished Judgement of Solomon, long given to Giorgione and now increasingly to Sebastiano.

He was a still-life painter in Toledo until 1603, when he left secular life to become a lay brother at the Carthusian monastery in Granada. The religious works he painted afterwards are unexceptional; as a still-life painter he ranks with the great names of European art.

Characteristically he shows a few simple fruits or vegetables arranged on a ledge with an almost geometric clarity, standing out against a dark background. Each form is scrutinised so intensely that the pictures take on a mystical quality — a feeling of wonder and humility in front of ordinary things.

After working in a Mannerist style he became one of the closest and most gifted of Caravaggio's followers — and one of the few who were actually friends of the master; in 1603 the two of them and two other artists were sued for libel by a rival painter.

His work has neither the power nor the uncompromising naturalism of Caravaggio's, tending instead towards the lyrical and refined: graceful, stately figures, clearly disposed, with sharp-edged drapery that recalls his Tuscan background. His daughter Artemisia trained with him and painted nothing like him.

In his lifetime he was known chiefly as a political and social satirist; since his death he has been increasingly recognised as a painter. Having learned the still fairly new process of lithography, he began contributing political cartoons to an anti-monarchist weekly in 1830.

He was an ardent Republican and in 1832 was given six months' imprisonment for his attacks on King Louis Philippe, whom he had drawn as Gargantua swallowing bags of gold extorted from the people. When the government banned political caricature in 1835 he turned to social satire instead.

Active almost his whole career in Bruges, where he had settled by 1484 and became the leading painter after Memling's death in 1494. The economic importance of the city was declining by then, but its prestige as a centre of art held up, and David played a large part in the flourishing export trade in paintings it developed in the early sixteenth century.

Swiss-born and active mainly in England, where he was one of the outstanding figures of the Romantic movement. He was a portrait painter's son but trained as a Zwinglian minister, taking holy orders in 1761 and abandoning the priesthood soon after.

He moved to London in 1764 on the suggestion of the British ambassador in Berlin, who had been impressed by his drawings. Reynolds encouraged him to take up painting, and he spent 1770 to 1778 in Italy engrossed in Michelangelo, whose elevated style he tried to match for the rest of his life.
An outstanding, if obscure, Antwerp still-life painter. She is no relation to the Peeters family of Antwerp marine and still-life painters she is sometimes filed alongside.

Generally taken for French, but his parents were English and he remained a British citizen all his life, twice trying unsuccessfully to naturalise. His father was a businessman who spent much of his life in Paris, and Sisley was headed for a commercial career before he turned to painting.

He entered Gleyre's studio in 1862 and met Renoir, Monet and Bazille there, forming the early nucleus of the Impressionist group. Like Monet he gave himself almost entirely to landscape, though his work was much less varied.

The leading portraitist of his day, the first president of the Royal Academy, a major theorist, and perhaps the most important figure in the history of British painting — because through his social and intellectual standing he raised the profession itself to a new level of dignity.
He was the son of a scholarly clergyman and grew up in an atmosphere of learning. He said he owed his first fondness for art to a treatise on the theory of painting that he read as a boy.
He died at twenty-six or twenty-seven and brought about a revolution in painting in that time, ranking with his friends Alberti, Brunelleschi and Donatello as a founding father of the Renaissance.

His nickname translates roughly as Hulking Tom or Sloppy Tom, given him, Vasari says, because he was so completely absorbed in art that he would give no time to worldly matters, down to the way he dressed. He joined the Florentine painters' guild in 1422, and nothing is known of his training.

Named after his birthplace in the Marches. He carried out important commissions in several major Italian centres and was recognised as one of the foremost artists of his day, but most of the work his contemporary reputation rested on has been destroyed — including frescos in the Doges' Palace in Venice and in St John Lateran in Rome.
His major surviving work is the Adoration of the Magi of 1423, painted for a Florentine church.

One of the outstanding Italian artists of his period, and Leonardo's master. His nickname means 'true eye', though it refers not to his sharpness of vision but apparently to a goldsmith he worked for early on.

He is said to have studied in Donatello's workshop, but his main training was as a goldsmith, and delicacy of craftsmanship is one of the salient features of his work. Only one piece in precious metal by him survives. His major activity was sculpture.

Prix de Rome in 1845, and with Bouguereau one of the most successful and influential academic painters of the period — and one of the sternest opponents of the Impressionists. The Birth of Venus is his best-known work and typical of the slick, titillating, supposedly chaste nudes he excelled at.

It was the hit of the official Salon of 1863, the year of the Salon des Refusés, and was bought by Napoleon III, who gave him several prestigious commissions afterwards. His reputation faded quickly once he was dead.

One of the greatest masters of still life and genre there has been. His forenames were traditionally given as Jean-Baptiste-Siméon, but the 'Baptiste' appears to have been a scribe's error and Jean-Siméon is now the accepted form.

He was Boucher's contemporary and briefly taught Fragonard, but his work contrasts with theirs in every way: it represents the naturalistic strain in eighteenth-century French art, influenced by seventeenth-century Dutch painting, that ran alongside the more fashionable Rococo. Almost all his pictures are modest in size and simple in subject.

One of the leading pupils of Gros, he won European fame with melodramatic, almost Hollywood-like history scenes; engravings of them hung in thousands of homes. He often took subjects from English history — Cromwell gazing at the body of Charles I, the Princes in the Tower, the execution of Lady Jane Grey.
The pictures are Romantic in flavour but academically impeccable in their drawing and detail. They went completely out of fashion for a long period afterwards.

In 1863 he led a revolt of fourteen students at the St Petersburg Academy, who walked out together because they thought its approach was out of touch with modern life. In 1870 they formed the nucleus of the Wanderers, of which he was a leading light.

He was a sensitive and highly principled man who held that only a sense of social purpose could give an artist strength, and only the confidence that the work was needed and appreciated by society could help those exotic plants called pictures to ripen.
His real name was Andrea d'Agnolo; the epithet 'del sarto', of the tailor, comes from his father's trade.

An animal painter, trained by her father and precociously gifted — she first showed at the Paris Salon at nineteen. In 1853 The Horse Fair was an enormous hit there, and repeated its success touring Britain and the United States.

She became well known as much for her character as her work: a colourful and formidable figure, outspoken in her independence, who drew at horse auctions and obtained police permission to wear men's clothes in order to do it.

He evidently spent his early career in Haarlem, but every documented work was made in Louvain, where he is first recorded in 1457 and was city painter from 1468. His major commissions there were a Last Supper altarpiece and two panels on the Justice of Emperor Otto for the town hall, left incomplete when he died.
Beyond those there are no documented works, but his manner is distinctive enough to identify — most obviously in the stiff, solemn, exaggeratedly elongated figures.

The greatest French painter of the fifteenth century, equally outstanding as a panel painter and a manuscript illuminator — the work in both fields has the same clarity, gravity and magnificent purity of line.

Little is known of his life, but his sober bearing is recorded in a remarkable miniature self-portrait painted in gold on black enamel, one of the earliest independent self-portraits that can certainly be identified — his name is boldly inscribed on it. Nearly everything else attributed to him rests on style and circumstance rather than documents.

Best known for luxurious flower pieces, but he made many other kinds of work, including group portraits that are important historical documents of his friendships among the avant-garde. Homage to Delacroix shows him with Baudelaire, Manet and Whistler around a portrait of Delacroix; A Studio at Batignolles shows Monet and Renoir in Manet's studio.

One of the most renowned society portraitists of his day, at his best with glamorous women — Sickert called it his wriggle-and-chiffon style. The vivacious brushwork and the knack of making sitters look graceful and poised recall his even more successful contemporary Sargent, and like Sargent his career was international: based in Paris from 1871, but travelling widely.
One of the dominant figures of late Victorian art. He travelled widely in Europe as a boy and got his artistic education principally in Frankfurt, Rome and Paris, not settling in England until 1859.

He had already made his name with a huge picture of Cimabue's Madonna carried in procession through the streets of Florence, painted in Rome, shown at the Royal Academy in 1855, and bought by Queen Victoria.
He began as an Impressionist, met Seurat in 1884, and became an ardent disciple of his views and method. After Seurat died in 1891 he was the acknowledged leader of the Neo-Impressionists.

In 1899 he published a book on the movement that was long treated as the authoritative account, though it is really more a manifesto in its defence than an objective history. It reflected his own turn towards more brilliant colour from about 1890, as he moved away from the scientific precision Seurat had insisted on.

Usually known as Girodet-Trioson, a name he took in honour of the surgeon who adopted him after he was orphaned young and who was probably his natural father. He studied with Jacques-Louis David, won the Prix de Rome in 1789, and spent five years in Italy.

In style and technique he followed David, but in his choice of subjects and the emotional charge he gave them he was Romantic. He was particularly drawn to unusual colour effects and melodramatic lighting.

Also called Mabuse, after Maubeuge, where he probably came from. He became a master in the Antwerp guild in 1503 and soon afterwards entered the service of Philip of Burgundy, in whose retinue he travelled to Rome in 1508–9 when Philip went as ambassador to the Vatican.
The work he made before that Italian journey belongs to the tradition of Hugo van der Goes. After it he settled somewhere in Zeeland, though nobody knows which town.

Active mainly in his native Iowa, and early on an artistic jack-of-all-trades. The turning point came with a commission for stained-glass windows in 1927, which took him to Munich the following year to supervise their manufacture.
The Early Netherlandish paintings he saw there changed his mind about how to paint. He dropped his earlier Impressionist manner for the meticulous, sharply detailed style of his mature work.

One of the most remarkable figures of the Romantic period and one of the supreme individualists in the history of art. He was equally gifted in poetry and the visual arts and worked in both in a highly original, deeply personal idiom that carried his idiosyncratic views and fiercely independent character.

His unorthodoxy was bound up with a hatred of materialism and rationalism, which he believed fettered the mind and spirit and led to misery and oppression. He was deeply religious and frequently painted Christian subjects.

The nickname Grien, green, perhaps refers to his liking for the colour. He probably trained with Dürer in Nuremberg, but his brilliant colour, expressive distortion and taste for the gruesome — he was fascinated by witchcraft — put him closer in spirit to Grünewald.
His output was varied and extensive: religious works, allegories and mythologies, portraits, designs for stained glass and tapestry, and a large body of graphic work, book illustration especially.

Regarded as the founder of the central tradition of Western painting, because his work broke decisively with the stylisations of Byzantine art, introduced new ideals of naturalism, and created a convincing sense of pictorial space.

His contemporaries knew what he had done — Dante praised him in a famous passage of the Divine Comedy, saying he had surpassed his master Cimabue — and to the generations after him it was plain that a new artistic era began with him.

One of the most original artists of his time, with links to Symbolism, a major influence on Expressionism, and claimed by the Surrealists as a forerunner — yet his work fits no school or group. His father was English and he held British nationality until 1929.

Apart from three years at the Brussels Academy and a few brief trips abroad he rarely left Ostend, where his parents kept a souvenir shop. The early works are mainly bourgeois interiors painted thickly and vigorously.

One of the most powerful and individual of the Expressionists. He began in a conservative, more or less Impressionist idiom and made a good living from it; serving as a medical orderly in the First World War changed both his outlook and his style completely.

He rarely painted the war itself, but the work afterwards is full of horrifying imagery, its forms expressively distorted in a way that reflects German Gothic art. Brutal realism and social criticism run together in it.

Nothing is recorded of his training. The early work shows Cranach, and he knew Dürer's woodcuts and engravings; mixed in with those German elements is a knowledge of Mantegna, perhaps at second hand. For all those influences his style stayed personal.
Most of his paintings are religious, but he was one of the first artists to treat landscape as a subject in its own right.

The leading artist of his day in Antwerp, where he became a master in 1491. His early career is obscure and his training a matter of guesswork: one early account says he was self-taught, another that he originally followed his father's trade as a blacksmith and took up art to win a sweetheart away from a painter she admired.
His first dated works are altarpieces of 1507–11, and in them he carries on the tradition of the great fifteenth-century Netherlandish masters.

One of the leading figures in Danish art in the first half of the nineteenth century, and sometimes called the father of Danish painting for the influence he had on his contemporaries. He trained in Copenhagen, then under Jacques-Louis David in Paris, then continued his studies in Rome.
He returned to Copenhagen in 1816 and was made a professor at the Academy two years later, where he revolutionised the teaching.

He evidently came from Siena, but all his known professional activity was in Florence. In 1391 he took vows as a monk of the Camaldolese monastery of S. Maria degli Angeli and rose to deacon; by 1402 he was enrolled in the painters' guild under his lay name and living outside the monastery. Lorenzo Monaco means 'Laurence the Monk'.
The monastery was renowned for its manuscript illumination and several miniatures have been attributed to him, but he was primarily a painter of altarpieces.

Named after the town he was born in, he worked mainly in nearby Venice, where he was one of the leading artists from about 1490 to 1510. His major works are almost all altarpieces, and he made numerous smaller pictures for private devotion, usually of the Virgin and Child.

Nothing is known of his training. His handsome, reflective manner changed very little across his career and was strongly marked by Giovanni Bellini, not least in the beautiful landscape settings — which has earned him the label 'the poor man's Bellini'.

The name means 'the red-headed Florentine'. Vasari says he would not bind himself to any master, which fits his temperament, but in his youth he learned most from Andrea del Sarto; with Andrea's pupil Pontormo, his friend and close contemporary, he was a leading figure in the early development of Mannerism.
His work was highly sophisticated and varied in mood, and he ended his career in France, at Fontainebleau.

He and his younger brother Piero ran a flourishing workshop together, in Florence and from about 1484 in Rome. Their surname means 'poulterer', evidently after their father's trade. Both are recorded as painters and sculptors and their individual shares are hard to disentangle, but Antonio was the dominant figure, and principally a goldsmith and worker in bronze.

The son of a retired ship's purser, he spent his early life on the Continent and trained partly in Antwerp. He settled in London in 1844 and was impressed by the Nazarenes on a visit to Rome soon after.

In 1848 he met Rossetti and through him joined the Pre-Raphaelite circle. He was never a formal member of the Brotherhood, but he shared their belief that art should be true to nature and morally edifying.

One of the most important of Caravaggio's followers in Rome. His life is poorly documented, but he probably settled there by about 1605 and could well have known Caravaggio personally, since the master left the city in 1606.

Most of his paintings take religious subjects, but he matters chiefly for his low-life scenes — taverns, card games, soldiers in guardrooms. It was Manfredi rather than Caravaggio himself who was mainly responsible for popularising that kind of picture.

His work is a diverse but highly personal response to European modernism. Stieglitz gave him a one-man exhibition in 1909 and helped him travel to Europe in 1912 — the start of the almost compulsive travelling that lasted the rest of his life. He was a lonely, reclusive, rather haunted man who never achieved much worldly success.
He lived in Europe until 1916, and in those years arrived at the distinctive semi-abstract manner he is best known for.

Remington, Frederic.name: Frederic Remington
Remington, Frederic.places: New York and the American West

context.text: The most famous portrayer of the Wild West. A burly, athletic man, he studied art at Yale and then travelled widely in the West, prospecting and cow-punching while he worked to establish himself as an illustrator.

Reproductions in Harper's Weekly and other popular journals made him a household name, and the success let him turn more to painting and sculpture. He settled in New York in 1885 but kept going back West.

Versatile and prolific, but remembered chiefly as the most important art teacher of his generation in America — at the Art Students League, at his own Chase School, and in Chicago and Philadelphia besides.

From 1891 he ran the Shinnecock Summer School on Long Island, the first important school of open-air painting in America, and he pioneered study trips abroad, visiting Europe regularly throughout his career.

A painter of imaginative subjects who lived most of his life as a solitary and a dreamer in New York, largely self-taught in both method and approach. The pictures reflect a rich inner life, with a haunting love of the sea — he was born in the fishing port of New Bedford.

He described the search that drove him: have you ever seen an inch worm crawl up a leaf or twig, and then, clinging to the very end, revolve in the air, feeling for something to reach? That, he said, was like him.
One of the pioneers of modernism in America. She belonged to the circle around Stieglitz, whom she met in 1916 and married in 1924.

She is best known for the near-abstract paintings built from enlarged flower and plant forms — elegant, rhythmically alive, and often sexually suggestive. In the 1920s she also painted New York townscapes close to the Precisionists, and landscapes in broad, simple forms.

One of the most attractive and idiosyncratic painters of the Sienese school. Little is known of his life, but a considerable number of works survive, all small religious panels, the earliest dated 1426.

He may have been taught by Taddeo di Bartolo and was notably influenced by Gentile da Fabriano and Sassetta, but the style is highly personal and engaging — rather whimsical figures inhabiting strange landscapes. His reputation revived after centuries of neglect.

The best-known exponent of Precisionism. Several trips to Europe between 1904 and 1909 gradually moved him off the bravura handling of his teacher Chase towards European modernism — the pictures he showed at the Armory Show in 1913 owe a great deal to Cézanne.
From 1912 he took up commercial photography for a living while continuing to paint, working for a while in fashion photography, to which his shy personality was not well suited.
He worked mainly in Missouri, where he also held several political posts, painting the life of the frontier people. Apart from a short spell at the Pennsylvania Academy he was self-taught.

His finest canvases distil a visual poetry out of the commonplace — Fur Traders Descending the Missouri above all. After a study visit to Düsseldorf in 1856–8 the work lost much of its racy freshness.
He grew up on a farm and is best known for sentimental scenes of rural life. Zola described the work as Impressionism corrected, sweetened and adapted to the taste of the crowd.

He was highly influential in spreading a taste for open-air painting — not only in France but in Britain, elsewhere in Europe, the United States and even, at second hand, Australia. He was much admired as a portraitist too.

One of the giants of the Renaissance and, in his later years, one of the forces that shaped Mannerism. His career lasted more than seventy years and for most of it he was the dominant figure in Italian art.

His contemporaries regarded him with something close to awe, and the word terribilità — terrifying intensity — was often applied to his work. He was the subject of two detailed biographies in his own lifetime, both written by people who knew him well.

Almost nothing is known of his life and only a handful of paintings can be confidently given to him, yet he holds a momentous place in the history of art. He had achieved legendary status soon after his early death, evidently from plague, and has gone on exciting the imagination in a way few painters can match.

The gap between his enormous fame and the tiny size of his surviving output is explained by what he began rather than what he left. He was among the earliest artists to specialise in cabinet pictures for private collectors rather than works for public or church patrons.

His nickname means 'Ox-head' or 'De-horner of oxen', which perhaps says something about his temperament. He was a contemporary of Dante, who in the Divine Comedy describes him as an artist believed to hold the field in painting, only to be eclipsed by the fame of Giotto.

A portrait painter, and the daughter of a pastellist from whom she had her first lessons. She was renowned for her beauty, wit and charm as well as for her talent, and had a highly successful career with many eminent sitters.
Queen Marie Antoinette was the most eminent of them; she painted her many times over, beginning in 1778.
He trained under Moretto in Brescia and worked mainly in Albino and nearby Bergamo, basing his style closely on his master's.

His religious paintings are unexceptional, but the portraits are worthy successors to Moretto's — remarkable for their psychological penetration, their dignified air, and an exquisite silvery tonality.

The friend and only documented pupil of Jacob van Ruisdael. Some of his pictures are very like Ruisdael's, but he was brighter in temperament and narrower in range, painting favourite subjects — watermills, trees around a pool — over and over again.

In 1668 he took a job with Amsterdam customs and excise, supervising the weighing and measuring of imported wine, and thereafter seems to have painted only in his spare time. His most famous work, The Avenue at Middelharnis, comes from those later years.

Early on he concentrated on scenes from the Greek and Roman world in a manner close to Alma-Tadema's, but in the 1880s he turned to literary themes — usually involving beautiful women — painted in a distinctive, dreamily romantic style.

In approach he owed a good deal to the Pre-Raphaelites, though his handling of paint is nothing like theirs: rich and sensuous where they were dry and precise. The Lady of Shalott is among the classic Victorian anthology pieces he produced.

The outstanding English portrait painter of his generation. He was a child prodigy and almost entirely self-taught, and he was handsome and charming besides; after an early triumph with his portrait of Queen Charlotte he never looked back, professionally or socially. The queen herself disliked the picture, but it was acclaimed at the Royal Academy.
On Reynolds's death in 1792 he succeeded him as official painter to George III, and he was elected a full Academician in 1794, at twenty-five.

He painted various subjects, but from the 1760s he specialised in still life, and is regarded as the finest Spanish painter in that field in the eighteenth century — sometimes called the Spanish Chardin. He spent much of his life in poverty. His work is rare outside Spain.

An enigmatic and exceedingly attractive artist, and nothing is known of his training or early career. He lived in Rome from about 1646 to about 1656 and there fell in with the Bamboccianti, painting genre scenes in their manner — but his are in a class apart, for the quiet, melancholy dignity of the figures and an exquisite tonality.
His Roman pictures also included views of artists' studios. He returned north by 1656, and died in Goa.
The dominant artist of Louis XIV's reign. He trained under Vouet and made a name for himself quickly, winning a commission from Cardinal Richelieu while barely out of his teens.
In 1642 he travelled to Rome in the company of Poussin, who was on his way back from a visit to Paris, and stayed there four years.
He ranks with Böcklin as the outstanding Swiss artist of his time, but the early work was unimaginatively naturalistic — landscapes amounting to ambitious colour postcards for tourists.
In 1890 that changed abruptly with Night, a brooding picture of a black-shrouded, phantom-like presence among semi-naked sleeping figures. It set the pattern for his most characteristic work.

The leading French painter of the first half of the seventeenth century. His early years are obscure, but an early biographer records him as precocious enough to be working as a portraitist in England at fourteen. He certainly visited Constantinople in 1611–12 before moving to Italy, where he lived from 1613 to 1627, mainly in Rome.
He built a considerable reputation there and became president of the Accademia di S. Luca in 1624. His early Italian work owes a great deal to Caravaggio.

A painter of genre scenes, portraits and still lifes, probably a pupil of Frans Hals in Haarlem. After marrying the painter Jan Miense Molenaer in 1636 she moved to Amsterdam, where the two shared a studio, using the same models and props.
She was one of Hals's best followers and her work has sometimes passed as his. Her monogram includes a star — a play on her name, which means lodestar.

The most famous member of a family of painters and now one of the most celebrated of all landscapists, though he painted many other subjects too. He was the son and probably the pupil of Jacob Gerritsz. Cuyp, and the early work also shows Jan van Goyen.
Closely associated with Dordrecht as he is, he seems to have travelled along the great rivers into the eastern Netherlands, and he painted views of Westphalia as well.

A painter and etcher of landscapes, and one of the most original and most enigmatic figures in the history of Dutch art. His name is now often spelled Seghers, but Segers is the form he and his contemporaries used.

Few details of his life are known. He was born in Haarlem, studied with Gillis van Coninxloo in Amsterdam, and worked in Utrecht and The Hague, where he is last mentioned in 1633; by 1638 the woman who was evidently his second wife is described as a widow.

A pioneer of still life and genre painting. He is best known for pictures that look at first glance like pure examples of either, but which turn out to have a religious scene worked into them — a butcher's stall, for instance, with the Flight into Egypt going on behind it.

One of the greatest Dutch still-life painters. He worked mainly in Antwerp, where he settled around 1635. The early pictures follow Balthasar van der Ast, and he also studied the restrained, simple work of the Haarlem still-life painters.

With Rachel Ruysch the most distinguished flower painter of his day. He had a European reputation and was much imitated, and his light colours and intricate, flamboyant compositions became characteristic of eighteenth-century Dutch flower painting.
He was a pupil of his father, Justus van Huysum the Elder, and occasionally painted something other than flowers — mainly landscapes.

Also called Jacob van Amsterdam, and the best-known member of a family of artists. He worked mainly in Amsterdam, where he was a successful painter and the leading designer of woodcuts of his period, among them a series illustrating Christ's Passion.

The Netherlands' most renowned painter of birds, who won an international reputation with vigorous, brightly coloured canvases showing domestic and exotic birds, often in violent movement and sometimes pointing a moral. He painted still lifes too, and was prolific. His father and grandfather were both painters before him.
One of the most celebrated of all still-life painters. He worked in Paris in the early 1640s and settled in Amsterdam in 1653. His early pictures are modest kitchen and courtyard scenes.

He became the outstanding exponent of a kind of still life in which fruit and precious objects — porcelain, oriental rugs, Venetian glass — are arranged in grand Baroque displays. He dealt in art as well as painting it.
A Netherlandish engraver and painter. The only evidence for his birth date of 1494 is an early biography, written long after the fact.

A painter of town views and architectural scenes, working in Haarlem, Amsterdam and The Hague. His pictures of those cities have documentary accuracy but are never dry — a subtle use of light and shade gives them a poetic harmony. His elder brother Job painted very similar work.

He became Rembrandt's pupil in Amsterdam around 1648 and stayed until 1653, when he went home to Dordrecht. His early work is genre painting, rather sentimental in approach but distinguished by the deep glowing colour he had learned from his master — old women sleeping, praying or reading the Bible were favourite subjects.
From the later 1650s he turned increasingly to portraiture, and from about 1660 he worked at it exclusively.
